chart.title: Athletes and officials allowed at the Youth Olympic Games

key_points: The chart compares how many athletes and officials may take part in the Summer and Winter Youth Olympic Games.
Summer athletes are by far the largest group, at 3,500.
Winter officials are the smallest group, at 580.
The Summer Games are much bigger: 3,500 athletes compared with 970 in winter, and 875 officials compared with 580.
In both Games athletes outnumber officials; in summer there are four athletes for every official.

chart.title: Sources of museum funding in the United States, 2009

key_points: The pie chart shows the four sources of funding for US museums in 2009.
Private or charitable giving was the largest source, at 36.5 percent.
Earned income came second with 27.6 percent, just ahead of government support at 24.4 percent.
Investment income was the smallest source, at 11.5 percent.
Private giving was more than three times investment income, and government support paid for less than a quarter of the total.

chart.title: Survey of over 10,000 US physicians: would they prescribe a placebo just because a patient wanted treatment?

key_points: The chart shows the results of a US survey of more than 10,000 physicians about prescribing a placebo simply because a patient wanted treatment.
Most doctors, 58 percent, said they would not do it.
24 percent said they would prescribe a placebo in this situation.
The remaining 18 percent, the smallest group, said it would depend on the circumstances.
Doctors who would not prescribe outnumbered those who would by more than two to one.

chart.title: Land taken over by urban expansion worldwide, 1992 to 2015

key_points: The chart shows how much land of each type was taken over as urban areas grew worldwide between 1992 and 2015.
Cropland was by far the biggest loss, at 24 million hectares.
Much less shrubland (4.6 million hectares) and forest land (3.3 million hectares, the smallest) were lost.
The cropland lost was more than five times the shrubland and more than seven times the forest land.
Together, these three types of land add up to about 32 million hectares lost to urban areas.

chart.title: Health facilities lacking basic services, 2015 (WHO and UNICEF estimates)

key_points: The chart shows the share of health facilities missing basic water and hygiene services, according to WHO and UNICEF estimates for 2015.
The biggest gap was water: 38 percent of facilities had no source of water.
35 percent had no means of handwashing, such as soap and water or hand rub.
The smallest figure was toilets: nearly 19 percent had none, about half the share without water.
Overall, more than a third of facilities had no water or no way to wash hands, and about one in five had no toilets.

chart.title: Share of world hydroelectricity generated by leading countries, 2022

key_points: The chart shows the shares of world hydroelectricity produced by five leading countries in 2022.
China was far ahead, producing 30 percent of the world total.
Brazil was second with 10 percent, just ahead of Canada at 9.2 percent.
The United States produced 5.8 percent and Russia the lowest share shown, 4.6 percent.
China's share was three times Brazil's and about the same as the other four countries combined.
Together, the five countries produced about 60 percent of the world's hydroelectricity.

chart.title: Adult obesity rate in selected countries, 2022

key_points: The chart compares adult obesity rates in five countries in 2022.
Tonga had the highest rate, 71.7 percent of adults.
The first four countries, Tonga, Nauru at 69.9, Tuvalu at 64.2 and Samoa at 62.4 percent, all had rates above 60 percent.
The United States had the lowest rate shown, 42 percent, almost 30 points below Tonga.
Even so, about two in five American adults are obese.

chart.title: Energy used per 100 passenger-kilometres by mode of transport, Japan, 1999

key_points: The chart compares the energy each mode of transport used per 100 passenger-kilometres in Japan in 1999.
Personal cars were the least efficient, using 68 kilowatt-hours.
Sea travel at 57 and air travel at 51 kilowatt-hours also used a lot of energy.
Public transport was far more efficient: buses used 19 and rail only 6 kilowatt-hours, the lowest.
A car used more than three times as much energy as a bus and more than eleven times as much as rail.

chart.title: Share of time spent awake in each 90-minute sleep cycle (one study of adults)

key_points: The line shows the percentage of time adults spent awake in each ninety-minute sleep cycle, in one study.
Awake time rose in every cycle, from 3 percent in the first to 12 percent in the fourth, four times as much.
The biggest increase came between the first and second cycles, from 3 to 8 percent.
After that the rise slowed, to 10 percent in the third cycle and 12 percent in the fourth.
Even in the fourth cycle, people were asleep for most of the time, about 88 percent.

chart.title: American adults who earned money in the platform economy, by activity, 2015

key_points: The chart shows the percentage of American adults who earned money in the platform economy in 2015, by type of activity.
Overall, about 24 percent of adults earned money in at least one of the three ways.
Selling something online was the most common activity, at 18 percent, nearly one in five.
8 percent, nearly one in ten, took on jobs or tasks through digital platforms, less than half the share who sold things online.
Renting out property on a home-sharing site was the least common, at only 1 percent.

chart.title: Global forest loss per year, 1990 to 2025

key_points: The chart compares yearly gross deforestation and net forest loss worldwide over three periods from 1990 to 2025.
Deforestation fell steadily, from 17.6 million hectares a year in 1990 to 2000, to 13.6 in 2000 to 2015, and 10.9 in 2015 to 2025.
Net forest loss dropped sharply, from 10.7 to 3.68 million hectares a year.
It then rose slightly, to 4.12 million hectares a year in 2015 to 2025, the only increase shown.
Net loss is always below deforestation because new forest growth is subtracted; the gap widened from about 7 to about 10 million hectares a year, then narrowed to under 7.

chart.title: Prices of recyclable cardboard and PET plastic, 2004 to 2009

key_points: The chart shows the prices of recyclable cardboard and PET plastic before and after the price collapse of 2008.
Both prices plunged in 2008 and then recovered strongly by May 2009.
PET plastic was always much more valuable: it averaged about 156 pounds per tonne, fell to 75, then rose to 195.
Cardboard averaged about 53 pounds per tonne, dropped to 19, then rose to 59.
By May 2009 both were above their 2004 to 2008 averages; cardboard lost almost two-thirds of its value in the fall, while PET roughly halved.

chart.title: Share of land needed for solar farms to supply 25 to 80 percent of electricity by 2050 (2021 study)

key_points: The table shows how much land solar panels would need to cover to supply 25 to 80 percent of electricity from solar farms by 2050, based on a 2021 study.
Japan and South Korea would need the largest share of their land, between 1.2 and 5.2 percent.
India would need the smallest share, only 0.3 to 1.4 percent.
The European Union falls in between, at 0.5 to 2.8 percent.
The upper estimate for Japan and South Korea is almost double the EU's and nearly four times India's, but even the highest figure is only just over 5 percent of land.

chart.title: Estimated number of species in selected groups

key_points: The table gives low and high estimates of the number of species in four groups.
Insects are by far the largest group, with 10 to 30 million species, and also have the widest range.
Bacteria come second, with 5 to 10 million species.
Fungi are estimated at 1.5 to 3 million species, and marine species at 0.7 to 1 million, the smallest estimate shown.
The high estimate is double the low one for bacteria and fungi and three times the low one for insects, which shows how uncertain these numbers are.

Honey bees are not the only bees that produce and store honey, but they form a small, distinct group. All true honey bees belong to one genus, or scientific group, called Apis. Today, scientists recognise just seven species of honey bee, which are divided into 44 subspecies. In the past, however, experts have recognised anywhere from six to eleven species. The study of bees, including honey bees, even has its own name: melittology.

Fossils show part of the history of honey bees. The first Apis bees appear in the fossil record of Europe about 34 million years ago, which shows that they were living there by that time. Scientists suspect that honey bees first came from South Asia, but very few fossil deposits are known from that region. In the Americas, there were no honey bees at all during human times until Europeans brought a species called Apis mellifera. Only one fossil species is known from there: a single 14-million-year-old bee found in Nevada.
key_points: Only members of the genus Apis are true honey bees, although some other bees also make and store honey.
There are just seven honey bee species (44 subspecies), though past counts ranged from six to eleven.
Apis bees first appear in Europe's fossil record about 34 million years ago.
Honey bees are thought to have come from South Asia, but few fossils are known from there.
There were no honey bees in the Americas in human times until Europeans brought Apis mellifera.

Both African and Asian elephants are endangered species. Elephants kept in captivity do not have many babies, and some of them are abused and treated badly.

African elephants have some legal protection in every country where they live. However, 70% of the land where they are found lies outside protected areas. In some places, conservation work has led to more elephants. Local numbers can be controlled with contraception or by moving elephants to other places. Large-scale culling, or legal killing, stopped in 1988, when Zimbabwe ended the practice.

In 1989, trade in elephants and their products, such as ivory and meat, was made illegal. In 1997, however, elephants in Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe were given a status that allows restricted trade, and South Africa's elephants received the same status in 2000. In some countries, hunting elephants for sport is legal. The IUCN estimated a total of around 440,000 African elephants for 2012.

There are about 40,000 to 50,000 Asian elephants, although this is only a rough estimate, and around half of them live in India. Their numbers are falling overall, especially in Southeast Asia, but the population in the Western Ghats may be increasing.
key_points: Both African and Asian elephants are endangered, and elephants in captivity have few babies and are sometimes mistreated.
African elephants have some legal protection in every country where they live, but 70% of their range is outside protected areas.
Conservation has increased elephant numbers in some areas; local numbers are controlled by contraception or moving elephants, and large-scale culling ended in 1988.
Trade in elephants and their products was banned in 1989, but restricted trade was later allowed in four countries, and sport hunting is legal in some countries.
About 440,000 African elephants were estimated for 2012; Asian elephants number roughly 40,000 to 50,000, about half of them in India, and are declining overall.

Tea is a caffeinated drink made by steeping the leaves of one plant, Camellia sinensis. Some other drinks, such as chamomile tea, are also called tea, but they are made by soaking herbs or fruit in hot water, and these are known as herbal teas. True tea comes in three main types: black tea, oolong and green tea. All three come from the same plant, but their leaves are treated in different ways.

For black tea, the leaves are broken into pieces and left in a room where they absorb oxygen. This is called oxidation, and the chemical reactions it causes change the taste and style of the tea. Oolong, a traditional Chinese tea, is only partly oxidized, and it is made by withering the leaves under strong sun. Green tea is different again. Freshly picked leaves are steamed, which keeps them green, and then they are crushed and dried in ovens.

In other words, the same leaves can become quite different teas, depending on how they are prepared.
key_points: True tea is a caffeinated drink made from Camellia sinensis leaves; herbal teas are made from other herbs or fruit.
There are three main types of tea (black, oolong and green), all from the same plant.
The types differ because the leaves are processed in different ways.
Black tea leaves are broken up and oxidized, which changes the taste; oolong is partly oxidized and withered in strong sun; green tea is steamed to stay green, then crushed and dried in ovens.

A team of scientists announced what they believed was the largest volcano on Earth. Called Tamu Massif, it lies about 2 kilometres below the sea on an underwater plateau known as the Shatsky Rise, around 1,600 kilometres east of Japan. The previous record-holder, Mauna Loa in Hawaii, was still the largest volcano on land.

Tamu Massif is enormous. It covers about 310,000 square kilometres, making it similar in size to Olympus Mons on Mars, the largest known volcano in the Solar System. It also extends about 30 kilometres into the Earth's crust.

The researchers concluded that it formed about 145 million years ago, when massive lava flows poured out from its centre and built a broad, shield-like shape. According to the researchers, this happened in a short time, geologically speaking: between one and several million years. They doubted that its peak ever rose above sea level, and they believed it had been extinct ever since, so it was unlikely to erupt again. Many ocean plateaus erupted between 145 and 65 million years ago, but none have appeared since, and scientists would like to know why.
key_points: Researchers described Tamu Massif, deep under the sea east of Japan, as Earth's largest volcano; Mauna Loa remained the largest on land.
It is enormous: about 310,000 square kilometres, similar in size to Olympus Mons on Mars.
Researchers concluded that it formed about 145 million years ago from massive lava flows, in a geologically short time.
Its peak probably never rose above sea level, and it is extinct and unlikely to erupt again.

Most earthquakes do not happen alone. Instead, they are part of a sequence of earthquakes that are linked to each other in place and time. Most of these groups, or clusters, are made up of small tremors that cause little or no damage.

Scientists give special names to the earthquakes in a sequence. A foreshock is an earthquake that happens before a larger one, called the mainshock. An aftershock comes after the mainshock, in the same place, and it is always smaller. Aftershocks happen because the Earth's crust is adjusting to the effects of the mainshock.

Some sequences follow other patterns. An earthquake swarm is a series of earthquakes that hit one area within a short time, but no single earthquake is clearly the main one. One example is the activity at Yellowstone National Park in 2004. In an earthquake storm, each earthquake is triggered by the ones before it, on nearby parts of a fault. Such storms can last for years, and the later earthquakes can be as damaging as the early ones. This happened on the North Anatolian fault in Turkey in the 20th century.
key_points: Most earthquakes happen in related sequences (clusters), usually made up of small, harmless tremors.
A foreshock comes before a larger mainshock; aftershocks follow in the same place, are always smaller and happen as the crust adjusts.
An earthquake swarm is a short burst of quakes in one area with no clear mainshock, such as Yellowstone in 2004.
In an earthquake storm, each quake triggers the next along a fault over years, as on Turkey's North Anatolian fault.

For a recycling programme to work, it needs a large and stable supply of recyclable material. Three kinds of legislation have been used to create such a supply: mandatory recycling collection, container deposit laws and bans on throwing away certain materials.

Mandatory collection laws set recycling targets for cities. Usually, they require a certain percentage of a material to be diverted from the city's waste stream by a target date, and the city itself is responsible for meeting this target.

Container deposit laws work in a different way. When people buy a product in certain containers, typically made of glass, plastic or metal, a small extra charge is added to the price. Consumers can get this money back by returning the container to a collection point. These programmes have achieved an average recycling rate of 80%. Despite such good results, they have faced strong opposition in some areas, because they shift the cost of collection away from local government and onto industry and consumers.

The third option is to ban the disposal of particular materials as waste, such as used oil, old batteries, tyres and garden waste. This can create a viable economy for disposing of these products properly. However, care must be taken to ensure that there are enough recycling services to handle the extra material; otherwise, such bans can lead to more illegal dumping.
key_points: A recycling programme needs a large, stable supply of recyclable material, and three kinds of law are used to create it.
Mandatory collection laws require cities to divert a set percentage of a material from waste by a target date.
Container deposit laws add a refundable charge to containers and average about 80% recycling, but face opposition because they shift costs to industry and consumers.
Bans on disposing of materials such as oil, batteries and tyres can build a proper disposal economy, but may increase illegal dumping if recycling services are lacking.

The timing of sleep is controlled mainly by two systems: the body's internal clock and a second mechanism called Process S, although personal choice also plays some part. The idea behind Process S is simple: the longer a person stays awake, the more they feel the need to sleep. This build-up is often called sleep debt.

One chemical sign of sleep debt is adenosine, a chemical messenger in the brain that suppresses many of the body's processes linked to being awake. Adenosine levels rise in parts of the brain during long periods of wakefulness and fall again while a person sleeps and recovers, so adenosine may act as a natural regulator of sleep. Coffee, tea and other sources of caffeine temporarily block its effect. They also make people take longer to fall asleep and reduce both the amount and the quality of their sleep.

Not getting enough sleep has clear costs. Sleep deprivation tends to shorten attention span, increase anxiety, weaken memory and put people in a grouchy mood. By contrast, a well-rested person tends to have better memory and mood.

However, much about sleep debt is still uncertain. Researchers disagree about how much of it can build up, and about what it should be measured against. There is some evidence that it is cumulative, yet people seem to feel sleepiest about 30 hours after waking up.
key_points: Process S means that the longer someone is awake, the stronger their need to sleep (sleep debt); it works with the body clock to time sleep.
Adenosine builds up in the brain during wakefulness and falls during sleep, so it may regulate sleep; caffeine blocks it and delays and worsens sleep.
Sleep deprivation shortens attention, raises anxiety and worsens memory and mood, while good rest improves memory and mood.
Much about sleep debt is still debated, such as how much can build up, though there is some evidence it is cumulative.

Most of the electricity produced around the world is used as soon as it is generated. This is because traditional power stations can adjust their output to match demand, and storing electricity is generally more expensive. Solar power, however, works differently. Like wind power, it is a variable source of energy, which means that all the power available at any moment must be used locally, sent elsewhere to be used, or stored, for example in a battery.

One key difficulty is that solar power is intermittent: it depends on both daylight and the weather, and it is not available at night. Storing it so that electricity is always available could therefore become an important issue, especially for systems that are not connected to the grid and for a future based entirely on renewable energy. For this reason, countries on the path to net zero that rely heavily on solar energy usually need to combine it with large-scale battery storage, pumped hydroelectric storage or long-distance transmission to keep the grid reliable.

On the positive side, solar output can be predicted to some extent from the time of day, the location and the season, although short-term generation still depends on the weather. The challenge of integrating solar power also varies greatly from place to place. In regions with hot summers and mild winters, for instance, solar tends to match daytime demand for cooling well.
key_points: Most electricity is used immediately, but solar is a variable source whose output must be used, transmitted or stored.
Solar is intermittent: it depends on daylight and weather and is unavailable at night, which makes storage important.
Countries relying heavily on solar for net zero need battery storage, pumped hydro or long-distance transmission to keep grids reliable.
Solar output is partly predictable, and the integration challenge varies by region; in places with hot summers and mild winters, solar matches daytime cooling demand well.

Vaccines are an essential part of the response to antimicrobial resistance. By preventing infections before they occur, they reduce the use and overuse of antimicrobial drugs and slow the emergence and spread of drug-resistant pathogens.

One important advantage is that microorganisms usually do not develop resistance to vaccines. This is because vaccines reduce the spread of infection and target a pathogen in several ways within the same host, and possibly in different ways in different hosts. There is also evidence that as vaccine use increases, antibiotic-resistant strains of pathogens decrease, because fewer infections mean less need for antibiotics. Vaccinated people are also protected against complications from secondary infections, which might otherwise require antimicrobial medicines or a stay in hospital.

The potential benefits are large. A 2024 report by the World Health Organization found that vaccines against 24 pathogens could reduce the number of antibiotics needed each year by 22%. If vaccines were rolled out against all the pathogens evaluated, they could save a third of the hospital costs associated with antimicrobial resistance.

Vaccines are not a perfect solution, however. Cases of vaccine resistance are well documented, although they are usually much less of a problem than antimicrobial resistance. In addition, vaccines against Staphylococcus bacteria have so far shown limited effectiveness, and more effective ones are still being developed and tested.
key_points: Vaccines are essential against AMR because preventing infections reduces antimicrobial use and slows the spread of resistant pathogens.
Microbes rarely become resistant to vaccines, since vaccines attack pathogens in several ways.
A 2024 WHO report found vaccines against 24 pathogens could cut antibiotic needs by 22% a year and could save a third of AMR-related hospital costs.
Vaccines have limits: vaccine resistance exists (though it is less serious), and anti-Staphylococcus vaccines have shown limited effectiveness.

Although urbanization tends to have more negative effects, it appears to have one clear benefit: people in cities are generally more physically active than people in the countryside. In the United States, rural residents have higher rates of obesity, get a larger share of their calories from fat and are less likely to meet the guidelines for physical activity. By contrast, metropolitan and large urban areas in every region have the highest levels of physical activity.

Several features of rural life help to explain this difference. Geographic isolation, busy and unsafe roads and social stigmas all reduce exercise. Because speed limits on rural roads are high, it is often impossible to have bike lanes, sidewalks or footpaths beside them, and there are fewer developed open spaces such as parks and trails. Many rural residents must also travel long distances to reach exercise facilities or their workplaces, which leaves less time for leisure activity and makes it harder to walk or cycle to work.

Urban environments, on the other hand, make activity easier. Residents of neighbourhoods with nearby fitness venues, sidewalks, street lights and traffic signals are more active than those in areas without such features. When many destinations are close to home, people walk and cycle more, and easy access to public transport also encourages them to walk or bike to the stops. It has therefore been argued that rural communities need more convenient recreational features.
key_points: One positive effect of urbanization is that city residents are more physically active than rural residents.
In the US, rural residents have more obesity, eat more fat and meet activity guidelines less often.
Rural barriers include isolation, unsafe roads, a lack of sidewalks, parks and trails, and long travel distances.
Urban features such as nearby fitness venues, sidewalks, close destinations and public transport encourage activity, so rural areas need more convenient recreational features.

Ocean acidification is not a new phenomenon. It has occurred several times in Earth's history, and it appears to have played a part in some of the most severe crises for life on the planet. Episodes of acidification took place during the Capitanian mass extinction, at the end of the Permian and Triassic periods, and during the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event. Indeed, three of the 'big five' mass extinctions were associated with a rapid rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide, probably caused by volcanic activity, the heat-driven breakdown of marine gas hydrates, or both.

The end-Triassic crisis remains the best-established example of a marine mass extinction caused by acidification, for two reasons. First, carbon isotope records point to increased volcanic activity that lowered carbonate saturation, and a marine extinction coincides precisely with this in the rock record. Second, the extinction selectively affected organisms with thick aragonite skeletons, just as experimental studies predict. Nevertheless, past extinction events were probably caused by several climatic stressors acting together, with acidification as only one of them.

The most notable example of acidification, however, is the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, about 56 million years ago, when massive amounts of carbon entered the ocean and atmosphere, causing carbonate sediments to dissolve across many ocean basins. New geochemical methods suggest that ocean pH fell by 0.3 units during this event. Yet one study indicates that carbonate saturation may have changed little, implying that carbon was released far more slowly then than it is by human activity today. Stronger methods are still needed to judge how much calcifying organisms were affected.
key_points: Ocean acidification has happened before and is linked to several mass extinctions; three of the big five involved rapid CO2 rises, probably from volcanism or gas hydrates.
The end-Triassic extinction is the best-established case, supported by matching carbon isotope and extinction records and the selective loss of organisms with thick aragonite skeletons.
Past extinctions were most likely driven by several climatic stressors together, with acidification as one factor.
The PETM, about 56 million years ago, is the most notable example (pH fell by about 0.3 units), but one study suggests its carbon release was much slower than today's human emissions.

The practice of doctors prescribing placebos disguised as real medication is controversial. The chief objection is that it is deceptive and could damage the relationship between doctor and patient in the long run. Some argue that blanket consent, a general agreement to unspecified treatment given by patients in advance, is ethically acceptable. Others insist that, out of respect for patient autonomy, people should always be told the name of the drug they are receiving, its side effects and the other treatment options available. Critics raise further concerns: doctors and pharmacists who use placebos could face charges of fraud or malpractice, and relying on placebos may delay the proper diagnosis and treatment of serious conditions.

Despite these objections, surveys suggest that many health professionals are willing to use placebos. In an Israeli study, 60% of the physicians and head nurses surveyed reported using them, and only 5% believed their use should be strictly prohibited. In the United States, a survey of more than 10,000 physicians found that 24% would prescribe a placebo simply because a patient wanted treatment, while 58% would not and 18% said it would depend on the circumstances.

Instead of deceiving patients, some writers propose a different approach. In his 2008 book Bad Science, Ben Goldacre argues that doctors should use the placebo effect to enhance medicines that actually work, and Edzard Ernst similarly suggests that a good doctor can transmit a placebo effect through the compassion shown to patients. Both, however, reject the idea that the placebo effect justifies alternative medicine, with Ernst warning that this would be deceitful and that the placebo effect is unreliable.
key_points: Prescribing disguised placebos is controversial, mainly because it is deceptive and may harm the doctor-patient relationship.
The concerns include consent and patient autonomy, possible fraud or malpractice charges, and delayed diagnosis of serious conditions.
Surveys nevertheless show that many health professionals are willing to use placebos (60% in an Israeli study; 24% of US physicians would prescribe one just because a patient wanted treatment).

Instead of deception, Goldacre suggests using the placebo effect to boost effective medicines and Ernst suggests passing it on through compassion, but both reject it as a justification for alternative medicine.

The question of when plate tectonics began on Earth has been the subject of considerable controversy. Estimates vary so widely between researchers that, taken together, they span about 85% of the planet's history.

Part of the disagreement concerns conditions on the early Earth. Some authors argue that, for at least part of the Archean period, roughly 4 to 2.5 billion years ago, the mantle was between 100 and 250 °C hotter than it is today. Such temperatures are thought to be incompatible with modern-style plate tectonics, suggesting that Earth may instead have had a so-called stagnant lid or some other kind of regime.

Other evidence, however, comes from ancient rocks. Rocks preserved from between 3 and 2.5 billion years ago become increasingly felsic in composition, which implies that subduction zones had emerged by then, and preserved zircons suggest that subduction may have begun as early as 3.8 billion years ago. Even so, these early subduction zones seem to have been temporary and localized, although how far this was true is itself debated.

Opinions also differ widely over when modern plate tectonics appeared. One view holds that it had emerged by at least 2.2 billion years ago. Other researchers argue that modern-style plate tectonics did not appear until 800 million years ago, pointing to the late appearance of rock types such as blueschist, which require cold subducted material. At the other extreme, some suggest that plate tectonics was already operating in the Hadean, over 4 billion years ago.
key_points: When plate tectonics began on Earth is highly controversial, with estimates spanning about 85% of Earth's history.
A much hotter Archean mantle may have been incompatible with modern-style plate tectonics, suggesting a stagnant lid or another regime.
Rock and zircon evidence suggests subduction had begun by 3 to 2.5 billion years ago, possibly by 3.8 billion, though early subduction zones seem to have been temporary and localized.

Estimates range from plate tectonics already working in the Hadean (over 4 billion years ago) to modern plate tectonics emerging by 2.2 billion years ago, or not until 800 million years ago (blueschist evidence).

In 1979, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published a paper called 'Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision Under Risk', which used cognitive psychology to explain various ways in which economic decisions depart from neo-classical theory. From their work, they drew three general conclusions: people treat gains differently from losses, they give too much weight to outcomes that are certain compared with those that are uncertain, and the way a problem is structured can affect the choices they make.

Part of the support for these claims came from a simple change to a survey question. When the question was reworded so that it was about avoiding losses rather than achieving gains, most respondents changed their answers. This suggested that emotions such as greed or the fear of loss can alter decisions, revealing an irrational element in the decision-making process.

According to prospect theory, choices are made in two stages. In the first, the editing stage, risky situations are simplified using various mental shortcuts, or heuristics. In the second, the evaluation stage, the risky alternatives are judged according to several psychological principles. Decision makers compare each outcome with a reference point, classifying results above it as gains and those below it as losses. They are also loss averse: in a later paper, published in 1992, Kahneman and Tversky estimated that a loss feels about 2.25 times as bad as an equal gain feels good. In addition, people tend to overweight small probabilities and underweight large ones, and they become less sensitive to further gains and losses as these grow larger.
key_points: Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 prospect theory used cognitive psychology to explain how real decisions under risk depart from neo-classical theory.
It holds that gains and losses are treated differently, certain outcomes are overweighted, and the way a problem is framed affects choices.
Rewording a survey question from gains to losses changed most answers, suggesting that emotions such as fear of loss can alter decisions.

Decisions involve an editing stage (simplifying with heuristics) and an evaluation stage based on reference points, loss aversion (losses hurt about 2.25 times more), probability weighting and diminishing sensitivity.

items.text:
Not all bilingual people can speak both of their languages. Receptive bilinguals are people who can understand a second language but cannot speak it, or whose ability to speak it is held back by psychological barriers.

This pattern is common among adult immigrants to the United States who do not speak English as a native language but whose children do, usually in part because the children have been educated in English. Although such parents understand both their native language and English, they speak only their native language to their children. If the children are themselves receptively bilingual but speak only English, the parents will use their native language throughout a conversation while the children reply in English. If the children can speak both languages, however, they may answer in their parents' language, in English or in a mixture of the two, depending on factors such as the content, context and emotional intensity of the conversation.

Receptive bilingualism need not be permanent. Receptively bilingual people, especially children, may quickly become fluent speakers if they spend long periods in situations where they must speak the language they previously understood only passively. Even before both generations are fluent, the language differences between them often cause little or no difficulty for the way the family functions.

Finally, receptive bilingualism should not be confused with mutual intelligibility. Mutual intelligibility, as between Norwegian and Swedish, is a property of a pair of languages that are objectively very similar in vocabulary and grammar. Receptive bilingualism, by contrast, is a property of individuals, shaped by how prominent each language has been in their upbringing, education and surrounding culture.
key_points: Receptive bilinguals understand a second language but cannot speak it, or are held back by psychological barriers.

It is common in US immigrant families: the parents understand English but speak only their native language, while their English-educated children reply in English or, if they speak both languages, in either language or a mix.
Receptive bilinguals, especially children, can quickly gain fluency when they must speak the language, and the generational difference rarely harms family life.
It differs from mutual intelligibility: receptive bilingualism belongs to individuals, whereas mutual intelligibility belongs to similar languages such as Norwegian and Swedish.

items.script: Today I want to talk about how a penguin's body suits its life. Penguins come in very different sizes. The biggest, the emperor penguin, can stand about one hundred and ten centimetres tall, while the smallest, the little penguin, is only about thirty-two centimetres tall. To stay warm, penguins have a thick layer of blubber, a kind of fat, and their feathers are packed very tightly. Under the outer feathers there is a layer of soft, woolly feathers, and the outer feathers are coated with oil that makes them waterproof. On land, penguins cannot walk well, so they waddle, and they cannot fly. Their wings have become small, stiff flippers. In the water, however, they use these flippers to swim very well. They also have webbed feet and good hearing, and they can see underwater.
key_points: Penguins vary a lot in size, from the emperor penguin (about 110 cm) to the little penguin (about 32 cm).
A thick layer of blubber and tightly packed feathers keep them warm.
Soft woolly down lies under the outer feathers, which are coated with oil that makes them waterproof.
On land they cannot walk well (they waddle) and cannot fly; their wings have become small, stiff flippers.
In water they swim very well using their flippers; they also have webbed feet and good hearing, and can see underwater.

items.script: Today I want to talk about chocolate and our health. Is chocolate good or bad for us? The answer is that it can be both. Chocolate is safe to eat, unless it is eaten in large amounts. But there are some exceptions. Some animals, such as dogs and cats, become sick even if they eat only a little chocolate. People with diabetes also need to be careful, because most chocolate has sugar added. On the other hand, chocolate can be good for us too. Dark chocolate contains ingredients that lower blood pressure and help to fight diseases. In fact, small amounts of dark chocolate have been found to lower the risk of heart disease, because of natural substances in chocolate called polyphenols. So the lesson is simple. We need to control how much chocolate we eat.
key_points: Chocolate is safe to eat unless it is eaten in large amounts.
Some animals, such as dogs and cats, get sick from even a little chocolate.
People with diabetes also need to be careful with chocolate because of its added sugar.
Dark chocolate has benefits: it contains ingredients that lower blood pressure and fight disease, and small amounts lower the risk of heart disease because of polyphenols.
The overall message is that people should moderate how much chocolate they eat.

items.script: Today I want to talk about the Olympic Games of ancient Greece. Their origin is surrounded by mystery. According to legend, Heracles first called the Games Olympic and started the custom of holding them every four years. The most widely accepted starting date is seven hundred and seventy-six BC, based on records of the winners of a footrace. The Games featured running, boxing, wrestling, horse events and the pentathlon, as well as chariot races. During the Games, conflicts between the Greek city-states were put on hold. Historians do not agree on when the ancient Games ended, but many believe it was in three hundred and ninety-three AD, when a Christian Roman emperor ordered an end to pagan religious practices. The Games were not held again until the late nineteenth century.
key_points: The origin of the ancient Olympics is uncertain and mixed with legend; Heracles is said to have named them and started the four-year custom.
The accepted starting date, 776 BC, is based on records of the winners of a footrace.
Events included running, boxing, wrestling, horse events, the pentathlon and chariot racing.
Conflicts between the Greek city-states were postponed while the Games took place.
The end date is disputed; many historians say 393 AD, when a Christian Roman emperor banned pagan practices, and the Games did not return until the late nineteenth century.

items.script: Let's talk about the phases of the Moon. The Moon does not make its own light. Because it is round, half of it is lit by the Sun, and we only see the parts that are lit. As the Moon travels around the Earth, we see different amounts of this lit side, from all of it to just a small part. These stages are called the phases of the Moon. The cycle starts with the new Moon, when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun. After that, we see more and more of the lit side each night until the full Moon, when the Moon and the Sun are on opposite sides of the Earth. Then the lit part we can see gets smaller again. The whole cycle takes about a month, and people throughout history have used it to measure time.
key_points: The Moon gives off no light of its own; the Sun lights half of it and we see only the lit parts.
As the Moon orbits the Earth, the amount of the lit side we can see changes; these stages are the phases.
The cycle begins with the new Moon, when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun.
After the new Moon, the lit part we can see grows until the full Moon (Moon and Sun on opposite sides of the Earth), then shrinks again.
A full cycle takes about a month, and people have used it throughout history to measure time.

items.script: Let's look at why rainforests are in danger. Rainforests were once so large and thick that few people lived there, but that is changing. Millions of poor people live nearby, and many hope to find a better life in the forest. Roads built by logging and mining businesses, and by governments, now reach deep into the jungle. Settlers use these roads to move in and burn the trees to make fields. But the soil is poor, so crops grow for only a few years. Then they sell the land to cattle ranchers, or clear more forest. Because so many farmers do this, no forest is left to grow back. Forcing them to stop would not help, because they would starve. Instead, new ways must be found for people to live on the land without destroying it.
key_points: Rainforests used to have few people, but millions of poor people nearby now move in hoping for a better life.
Roads built by businesses (cutting trees, digging minerals) and by governments let settlers into the forest.
Settlers burn the forest for fields, but the poor soil grows crops for only a few years; then the land goes to cattle ranchers or more forest is cleared.
Because so many farmers do the same, the forest cannot grow back.
Forcing farmers to stop would not work because they would starve; new ways are needed to live on the land without destroying it.

items.script: Today I want to look at how climate change is affecting glaciers. Since the industrial era, human activities have added carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases to the air, causing global warming. Human influence is now the main driver of change in the frozen parts of our planet, including glaciers. One problem is that warming and melting feed each other. Melting glaciers expose more land and sea, which are darker than ice. So instead of being reflected back into space, sunlight warms these surfaces, and this leads to even more melting. The reference glaciers tracked by the World Glacier Monitoring Service have lost ice every year since nineteen eighty-eight. Water running off melting glaciers also raises sea levels, which threatens coastal towns, small islands and coastal ecosystems, and can make groundwater salty. Switzerland shows the cost. In twenty twenty-three, it lost four percent of its glacier volume, and it reportedly spends close to five hundred million dollars a year protecting Alpine settlements.
key_points: Greenhouse gases from human activity since the industrial era cause global warming, and human influence is now the main driver of glacier change.
Melting and warming reinforce each other: exposed land and sea are darker than ice, absorb sunlight and cause more melting.
The reference glaciers tracked by the World Glacier Monitoring Service have lost ice every year since 1988.
Glacier meltwater raises sea levels, threatening coastal settlements, small islands, coastal ecosystems and groundwater (salinisation).
Switzerland shows the cost: it lost 4% of its glacier volume in 2023 and spends about 500 million US dollars a year protecting Alpine settlements.

items.script: Today I want to talk about the damage that hydroelectric dams can do to the environment. The first problem is the loss of land. A large dam creates a large reservoir, which floods wide areas upstream and can destroy rich forests, marshes and grasslands. Building large dams also often means moving people and wildlife away, and the reservoir can break up the surrounding habitats, which makes the loss even worse. The second problem is the effect on the river itself. A dam interrupts the river's natural flow, and this can harm ecosystems both upstream and downstream. For example, the water that comes out of a turbine carries very little sediment, so it can wear away the river bed and the riverbanks. The turbines can also kill many of the animals that pass through them, such as eels. And because the turbine gates are often opened only from time to time, the river's flow can change quickly, sometimes every day.
key_points: Large reservoirs flood wide areas upstream, destroying rich forests, marshes and grasslands.
Building large dams often displaces people and wildlife, and reservoirs break up surrounding habitats, worsening the loss of land.
Dams interrupt the natural flow of rivers and can harm ecosystems both upstream and downstream.
Water leaving turbines carries little sediment and erodes river beds and banks; turbines also kill many animals passing through, such as eels.
Because turbine gates open only intermittently, river flow can change rapidly, even daily.

items.script: Today I want to talk about the Grand Tour, which is often seen as the beginning of modern tourism. The Grand Tour was a traditional trip around Europe, taken mainly by wealthy young men from the upper classes. It is most closely linked with the British nobility and rich landowning families, although young men from other northern European countries made similar trips. The custom flourished from about sixteen sixty until the eighteen forties, when large-scale rail travel arrived. The tour was seen as an educational opportunity and a rite of passage, and it became a status symbol for upper-class students. Because classical art was greatly admired at the time, the tour centred on France and especially Italy, where students could see rare examples of classical art and history. They could also mix with polite, aristocratic society on the continent. After that, railways and steamships made the journey easier, and the tradition spread to more of the middle class.
key_points: Modern tourism can be traced to the Grand Tour, a traditional trip around Europe.
It was taken mainly by wealthy upper-class young men, especially British nobles and landed gentry, and flourished from about 1660 until large-scale rail travel in the 1840s.
It was an educational opportunity, a rite of passage and a status symbol for upper-class students.
Because classical culture was admired, the tour centred on France and especially Italy, offering classical art and history and contact with aristocratic continental society.
Rail and steamship travel later made the journey easier and extended the tradition to more of the middle class.

items.script: Today I want to talk about a less obvious effect of deforestation, its link to infectious disease. When forests are cleared, many species disappear, and people are often exposed to zoonotic diseases, which are diseases that pass from animals to humans. Several diseases are associated with forests, including malaria, Lyme disease and Ebola. In fact, most new infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic, including the virus behind the coronavirus pandemic. Their emergence may be linked to habitat loss and to people moving into forest areas, because both increase human contact with wildlife. A second pathway is called range expansion. When forests are cut down, animals that carry diseases are forced into neighbouring habitats, and their pathogens can find new hosts there, including people. Deforestation has also been linked to more disease outbreaks. In Malaysia, for example, forest was cleared for pig farms, and this increased the spread of the Nipah virus. According to the World Economic Forum, thirty-one percent of emerging diseases are linked to deforestation.
key_points: Deforestation removes many species and exposes people to zoonotic diseases, which pass from animals to humans.
Many diseases are forest-associated (e.g. malaria, Lyme disease, Ebola), and most new human infectious diseases, including the virus behind COVID-19, are zoonotic.
Habitat loss and people moving into forests increase human contact with wildlife.
Through range expansion, displaced disease-carrying animals bring their pathogens to new areas where they find new hosts, including humans.
Deforestation is linked to outbreaks, e.g. clearing for pig farms in Malaysia spread the Nipah virus; the World Economic Forum links 31% of emerging diseases to deforestation.

items.script: Today I want to talk about how an inactive lifestyle is linked to obesity. First, where people live matters. Obesity risk has been linked to community design and to our reliance on cars. In one study around Atlanta, people in the most walkable neighbourhoods were two point four times more likely to get the recommended amount of physical activity than people in the least walkable areas. Second, work and daily life have become less active. Around the world, there has been a large shift towards less physically demanding jobs, and at least thirty percent of the world's population gets too little exercise. This is mainly because of the growing use of mechanised transport and labour-saving technology at home. Children also seem to be less active than before, especially in walking and physical education, although this may not be a significant cause of obesity in children. Finally, in both children and adults, time spent watching television is associated with the risk of obesity.
key_points: A sedentary lifestyle is linked to obesity risk.
Community design and car dependence matter: in an Atlanta study, people in the most walkable neighbourhoods were 2.4 times more likely to get enough physical activity.
A worldwide shift to less physically demanding work means at least 30% of people get too little exercise, mainly because of mechanised transport and labour-saving home technology.
Children appear less active than before (especially walking and physical education), though this may not be a significant contributor to obesity.
Time spent watching television is associated with obesity risk in both children and adults.

items.script: Let's look at what happens when our circadian rhythms, our internal daily clocks, are disrupted. The most familiar example is jet lag, which can cause fatigue, insomnia, headaches and loss of appetite. In the longer term, however, disruption is believed to seriously affect organs outside the brain. Researchers study this partly through shift workers, whose body clocks can fall out of step with day and night. The first concern is the heart. In one early study, hamsters with a genetically faulty body clock developed serious heart and kidney disease on a twenty-four-hour light and dark cycle that did not match their own rhythm. Shift workers have shown higher blood pressure and markers linked to plaque building up in their arteries. The second concern is metabolism. Animals forced to eat during their normal resting period gain weight, and in humans, shift work with irregular mealtimes is linked to diabetes and higher body mass. Finally, there are effects on the mind. Long-term shift workers make more errors, and night shift workers face a higher risk of dementia, especially those over fifty. So keeping normal sleep and daily rhythms matters for both brain and body.
key_points: Disrupting circadian rhythms generally harms health; jet lag is a short-term example (fatigue, insomnia, headaches, appetite loss).

Long-term disruption, studied partly in shift workers, is believed to harm organs outside the brain, especially the heart: clock-defective hamsters on a mismatched cycle developed heart and kidney disease, and shift workers show higher blood pressure and artery-plaque markers.
Misalignment affects metabolism: animals fed during their rest period gain weight, and irregular shift-work eating is linked to diabetes and higher body mass.
There are cognitive effects: chronic shift workers make more errors, and night shift workers have a higher dementia risk, especially over 50.
Maintaining normal sleep and circadian rhythms is important for brain and overall health.

items.script: Today I'd like to discuss why high or unpredictable inflation is seen as harmful to an economy. To begin with, it creates inefficiencies and makes it hard for companies to budget or plan for the long term. Uncertainty about what money will be worth in the future also discourages investment and saving. Next, inflation shifts purchasing power between groups. People on fixed incomes, such as pensioners whose pensions are not adjusted for rising prices, lose out to people whose earnings can keep pace with inflation. Inflation can also act as a hidden tax, because rising earnings push taxpayers into higher tax brackets unless those brackets are adjusted. There are also practical costs. When prices keep rising, people may hoard goods that last as a store of wealth, which creates shortages. Firms must change their prices often, which costs time and money, and this is called the menu cost. Holding cash also becomes more costly, so people keep more money in interest-paying accounts and make more trips to the bank, the so-called shoe leather cost. In extreme cases, hyperinflation can even lead people to abandon their country's currency for foreign ones.
key_points: High or unpredictable inflation is considered harmful: it creates inefficiency and makes long-term budgeting and planning difficult.
Uncertainty about the future value of money discourages investment and saving.
It redistributes purchasing power from people on fixed incomes (e.g. unindexed pensions) to those whose earnings keep pace, and can act as a hidden tax by pushing taxpayers into higher brackets.
It causes practical costs: hoarding and shortages, menu costs of frequent price changes, and shoe leather costs of extra trips to the bank.
In extreme cases, hyperinflation can make people abandon the national currency for foreign currencies.

items.script: Let's explore how young children work out what words mean. On average, children learn ten to fifteen new word meanings every day, but only about one of these comes from direct teaching. One proposal for the rest is that children rely on context. When they meet an unfamiliar word, they use the surrounding information to guess its rough meaning, and they usually guess correctly. Children also stretch words they already know to cover related things they have no word for. For instance, a child might use the word mummy for anything that belongs to their mother, or even for anyone who looks like their parents. A child might also say the word rain when they mean they don't want to go out. In addition, children seem to follow certain rules of thumb. They tend to assume that a word refers to objects with similar properties, so a cow and a pig can both be animals, rather than to things that go together, like a cow and milk. They also assume that a new label names a whole object, not one of its parts. These assumptions help, but they can sometimes lead to conflicting conclusions.
key_points: Children learn about 10 to 15 new word meanings a day, but only about one comes from direct instruction.
One proposal is that they use context to guess the rough meaning of unfamiliar words, usually correctly.
Children extend words they already know to related things they have no word for (e.g. mummy for anything belonging to their mother).
They use heuristics: assuming words refer to objects with similar properties rather than thematically related things, and that a new label names the whole object, not a part.
These assumptions help word learning, but conclusions based on them can sometimes conflict.

items.script: Today I want to look at the role of sewage treatment plants in microplastic pollution. These plants clean wastewater, mainly from homes, using physical, chemical and biological processes. In developed countries, most plants have two main stages. In the first, filters and settling tanks remove oils, sand and other large solids. In the second, bacteria and other tiny organisms break down organic matter. Some plants add a third stage, for example to disinfect the water. Microplastics have been found in both main stages, and the good news is that most are removed. One study estimated a removal rate of about ninety-nine point nine percent, with roughly one particle per litre released back into the environment. Another found that most particles are removed in the first stage. So when these plants work properly, they are not a disproportionately large source of microplastics. However, current technology cannot clean the water completely. There is also a second problem. In some countries, the leftover sludge is used to fertilise soil. There, weather and sunlight break the plastics into smaller pieces, and many end up in storm drains and eventually back in bodies of water.
key_points: Sewage treatment plants clean mostly household wastewater in stages: physical removal of large solids, then biological breakdown of organic matter, sometimes a third stage such as disinfection.
Microplastics occur in both main stages, but removal is very efficient (about 99.9%, mostly in the first stage), leaving roughly one particle per litre.
When working properly, the plants are not a disproportionately large source of microplastics in oceans and surface waters.
Current technology still cannot remove all microplastics from the water.
Sludge used as fertiliser exposes plastics to weather and sunlight, which fragment them; the pieces reach storm drains and eventually bodies of water.

items.topic: Game theory in economics and business
items.script: Today I'd like to explain how game theory is used in economics and business. Game theory is a major method in mathematical economics for modelling the behaviour of agents who interact and compete. It has been applied to many economic questions, including auctions, bargaining, mergers and acquisitions, and markets with only a few competing firms. Research in this area usually focuses on sets of strategies known as equilibria, and it commonly assumes that players act rationally. In non-cooperative games, the most famous is the Nash equilibrium. A set of strategies is a Nash equilibrium if each player's strategy is the best response to the others. In that case, no player has a reason to change strategy alone, because they are already doing the best they can, given what everyone else is doing. Game theory is also widely used in managerial economics to analyse strategic interactions between firms. It can help managers understand how their decisions affect competitors and the whole market. It can also be used to study cooperation, such as strategic alliances or joint ventures. Finally, firms can use it to choose the best pricing strategy, based on how they expect competitors to respond.
key_points: Game theory is a major method in mathematical economics and business for modelling interacting, competing agents, applied to auctions, bargaining, mergers and acquisitions, and oligopolies.
Research focuses on equilibria (solution concepts) and commonly assumes players act rationally.
In a Nash equilibrium, each player's strategy is a best response to the others', so no player gains by changing strategy alone.
In managerial economics it is used to analyse strategic interactions between firms, such as how decisions affect competitors and the market.
It also helps analyse cooperation between firms (strategic alliances, joint ventures) and pricing strategies based on expected competitor responses.

items.script: Different bicycles do different jobs. The city bicycle is made for errands and commuting in cities. It has a comfortable seat, lights, a bell and mudguards, but it is heavy. The rider sits upright, so steering in traffic is easy. The road bicycle has narrow wheels and a much lighter frame than a mountain bike, so it is efficient for longer distances. On a recumbent bicycle, the pedals are in front of the seat and the rider leans back. This is more comfortable for most people but costs more, and some types sit low to the ground, so they can be harder for other road users to see. The fastest bikes in the world are recumbents.
key_points: Different types of bicycles are designed for different purposes.
City bicycles are made for errands and commuting: they are comfortable but heavy, and the rider sits upright for easy steering in traffic.
Road bicycles have narrow wheels and a much lighter frame than mountain bikes, so they are efficient over longer distances.
On recumbent bicycles the pedals are in front of the seat and the rider leans back; this is more comfortable for most people but costs more, and low types can be harder for other road users to see.
The fastest bikes in the world are recumbents.

items.script: How is coffee grown? The traditional way is to put twenty seeds in a hole at the start of the rainy season. But about half of the seeds are wasted, because they do not sprout. Farmers in Brazil use a better method. They grow young plants in nurseries and move them outside after six to twelve months. Coffee is often grown with other food crops, such as corn, beans or rice, for a few years. This helps farmers learn what coffee plants need to grow well. Coffee grows between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, an area called the bean belt, or coffee belt.
key_points: The traditional method is to plant twenty seeds in a hole at the start of the rainy season, but about half of the seeds do not sprout and are wasted.
Farmers in Brazil use a better method: they grow seedlings in nurseries and move them outside after six to twelve months.
Coffee is often grown alongside food crops such as corn, beans or rice for a few years, which helps farmers learn what coffee plants need to grow well.
Coffee plants grow between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, an area called the bean belt or coffee belt.

items.script: Let's talk about baby elephants. A female elephant has a single baby, called a calf, every four or five years, and it grows inside her for about twenty-two months. Another female often stays with the mother until the baby is born. A newborn calf can often stand within half an hour. First, it wobbles around looking for its mother's milk, and it drinks about ten litres a day. Calves drink their mother's milk for their first two years. Mothers touch their babies gently with their trunks, but a calf needs a year or more to control its own trunk and learn its many uses.
key_points: A female elephant has a single calf every four or five years, after a pregnancy of about twenty-two months.
Another female often stays with the mother until the baby is born.
A newborn calf can often stand within half an hour, and the first thing it does is look for its mother's milk.
Calves drink about ten litres of milk a day and nurse for their first two years.
Mothers touch their calves gently with their trunks, but a calf needs a year or more to control its own trunk and learn its uses.

items.script: Why did the dinosaurs disappear? About sixty-six million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous period, a massive meteorite hit the Earth in the Yucatan peninsula, in what is now Mexico, and this caused mass extinctions. Other impact craters, and huge volcanic activity in India, date from about the same time. These events may have reduced sunlight and made it harder for plants to make food, which badly disrupted life on Earth. Did any dinosaurs survive? Yes, because birds are descended from dinosaurs. But dinosaurs as we usually think of them were wiped out. Some fossils have been found in later rocks, but many scientists believe these bones were washed out of their original places and buried again.
key_points: About 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous, a massive meteorite hit the Earth in the Yucatan peninsula in Mexico, causing the extinctions.
Other impact craters and massive volcanic activity in India date from about the same time.
These events may have reduced sunlight and made it harder for plants to make food, badly disrupting life on Earth.
Birds, which are descended from dinosaurs, survived, but dinosaurs as generally understood were wiped out.
Many scientists think dinosaur fossils found in later rocks were washed out of their original places and buried again.

items.script: The Internet is the world's largest communication network for computers and other devices. It was developed in the United States by a research agency of the Department of Defense, and it was first connected in October nineteen sixty-nine, under the name Arpanet. In nineteen ninety, a British scientist named Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web in Switzerland. Today, the Web is one of the Internet's most popular services, used by billions of people every day. People pay internet service providers to get online. Many websites are free to use, and some of them show advertisements to earn money. There are also ongoing debates about censorship and freedom of speech online.
key_points: The Internet is the world's largest communication network for computers and other devices.
It was developed in the United States by a Department of Defense research agency and first connected in October 1969, when it was called ARPANET.
In 1990, British scientist Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web in Switzerland; the Web is now one of the most popular services, used by billions of people every day.
People pay internet service providers for access; many websites are free, and some show advertisements to earn money.
There are ongoing debates about censorship and freedom of speech on the Internet.

items.script: Machines using wind to grind grain and pump water were developed by the ninth century. But when was wind first used to make electricity? In July eighteen eighty-seven, in Scotland, Professor James Blyth built a ten-metre wind turbine with cloth sails in the garden of his holiday cottage at Marykirk. It charged batteries that powered the cottage's lights, making it the first house in the world to get its electricity from the wind. Blyth offered his spare power to the people of Marykirk to light their main street, but they refused, believing electricity was the work of the devil. He later built a turbine to supply emergency power to a hospital in Montrose. However, the invention never really caught on, because it was not considered economically viable.
key_points: Wind machines for grinding grain and pumping water existed by the ninth century, but the first wind turbine for generating electricity was built in Scotland in July 1887 by Professor James Blyth.
His ten-metre, cloth-sailed turbine at his holiday cottage in Marykirk charged batteries that lit the cottage, making it the first house in the world powered by wind electricity.
The people of Marykirk refused his offer of spare power to light their main street because they thought electricity was the work of the devil.
Blyth later built a turbine to supply emergency power to a hospital in Montrose.
The invention never really caught on because it was not considered economically viable.

items.script: How does public transport shape cities? Dense areas with mixed land uses encourage daily public transport use, while urban sprawl is linked to only occasional use. A recent multi-city European survey found that density, reliable and affordable services, and limiting motor vehicles in high-density areas all help promote public transport. Urban space is precious, and public transport uses it more efficiently than cars, so cities can be built more compactly. If public transport planning is at the heart of city planning, it forces cities to be built compactly around stations and stops. Centres can then grow around these hubs, serving passengers' daily needs and public services, which greatly reduces sprawl. In contrast, poor land use and planning reduce people's access to jobs, education and health care.
key_points: Dense, mixed-use areas encourage daily public transport use, whereas urban sprawl is linked to only occasional use.
A European multi-city survey found that density, reliable and affordable services, and limiting motor vehicles in high-density areas help promote public transport.
Public transport uses scarce urban space more efficiently than cars, allowing cities to be built more compactly.

Putting public transport planning at the core of urban planning makes cities compact around stations and stops, creates centres around hubs for daily needs and public services, and greatly reduces sprawl.
Inefficient land use and poor planning reduce access to jobs, education and health care.

items.script: The purpose of museums has changed greatly over time. In the nineteenth century, museums focused on scientific research and on organising collections, often gathered through exploration and colonialism. They were mostly for scholars, but they began opening to the public to educate and improve society. In the early twentieth century, exhibits were mostly static and aimed at scholars, often valuing the objects above the visitor's experience. In the second half of the century, reduced government funding pushed museums to rely more on private support and attract visitors to earn money, so they turned to public engagement and interactive exhibits. Today, museums aim to be accessible and inclusive. They use virtual tours and online collections to reach wider audiences, and they have become spaces for discussion and social change.
key_points: In the nineteenth century, museums focused on scientific research and organising collections, often gathered through exploration and colonialism; they were mainly for scholars but began opening to the public to educate and improve society.
In the early twentieth century, exhibits were mostly static and aimed at scholars, often putting objects ahead of the visitor experience.

In the second half of the twentieth century, reduced government funding pushed museums to rely more on private support and on attracting visitors for revenue, so they shifted to public engagement and interactive exhibits.
In the twenty-first century, museums aim to be accessible and inclusive, using digital tools such as virtual tours and online collections to reach wider audiences.
Museums have also become spaces for discussion and social change.

items.script: How do bees turn nectar into honey? A foraging bee collects nectar, which is usually seventy to eighty percent water, in its honey stomach, where enzymes start breaking complex sugars into simpler ones. In the hive, it passes the nectar to hive bees. Working in relay groups, they repeatedly form bubbles of nectar between their jaws to evaporate water. This can take up to twenty minutes. The new honey is placed in honeycomb cells, but it is still so watery that yeast could grow in it. So the bees keep the hive warm with their body heat and beat their wings to move air across the honey. When the water content falls to fifteen point five to eighteen percent, fermentation stops, and the bees seal the cells with wax.
key_points: A forager bee collects nectar, usually 70 to 80 percent water, in its honey stomach, where enzymes begin breaking complex sugars into simpler sugars.
In the hive, the nectar is passed to hive bees, which work in relay groups and repeatedly bubble it between their jaws to evaporate water, for up to twenty minutes.
The new honey is placed in honeycomb cells while it is still watery enough for yeast to grow in it.
Bees keep the hive warm with their body heat and beat their wings to move air across the honey, drawing out water.
When the water content falls to 15.5 to 18 percent, fermentation stops and the bees seal the cells with wax.

items.script: Composting is an aerobic process, meaning it needs oxygen. It turns organic waste into a humus-like material that makes a good fertiliser. The organisms involved need four equally important ingredients. Carbon, typically from brown, dry materials, provides energy, and as microbes break it down, they produce the heat the process needs. Nitrogen, typically from green, wet materials, lets the organisms grow and reproduce. Oxygen is needed to break down the carbon, and water is needed in the right amount, without creating areas that lack oxygen. Turning the pile keeps the oxygen and moisture right. Composting works best at about twenty-five parts carbon to one part nitrogen. Above thirty to one, the pile lacks nitrogen, and below fifteen to one, some nitrogen is likely to escape as ammonia.
key_points: Composting is an aerobic process that turns organic waste into humus-like compost, a good fertiliser.
Composting organisms need four equally important ingredients: carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and water.

Carbon supplies energy and, as microbes break it down, heat; carbon-rich materials tend to be brown and dry. Nitrogen lets organisms grow and reproduce; nitrogen-rich materials tend to be green and wet.
Oxygen is needed to break down carbon, and water must be at the right level without causing oxygen-free conditions; turning the pile maintains oxygen and moisture.
The ideal carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is about 25 to 1; above 30 to 1 the pile is nitrogen-starved, and below 15 to 1 nitrogen is likely lost as ammonia.

items.script: Cognitive load theory has its roots in the beginning of cognitive science in the nineteen fifties. In a classic paper from nineteen fifty-six, Miller was perhaps the first to suggest that human working memory has inherent limits. His results suggested that people can generally hold only about seven units of information, plus or minus two, in short-term memory. In nineteen seventy-three, Simon and Chase used the term chunk to describe how people might organise information in short-term memory, a process also described as schema construction. Then, in the late nineteen eighties, Sweller developed cognitive load theory while studying problem solving. He and his colleagues found that learners often use a strategy called means-ends analysis, which uses up a lot of processing capacity, leaving less for building schemas. To prevent this unnecessary load, Sweller suggested designing instructional materials that avoid problem solving, such as worked examples and goal-free problems.
key_points: Cognitive load theory traces back to 1950s cognitive science: Miller's 1956 paper was perhaps the first to suggest that working memory has inherent limits, about seven units plus or minus two.
In 1973, Simon and Chase used the term chunk for how people organise information in short-term memory, a process also described as schema construction.
In the late 1980s, Sweller developed cognitive load theory while studying problem solving.
He found that learners often use means-ends analysis, which uses up a lot of processing capacity and leaves less for building schemas.
To prevent this unnecessary load, he recommended instructional materials that avoid problem solving, such as worked examples and goal-free problems.

items.topic: Gender pay gap in gig work
items.script: Is there a gender pay gap in the gig economy? The research is mixed, but many studies show that women still earn less than men on platforms, and the gap is typically similar to the gap outside the gig economy. One analysis of Uber drivers in the United States found that women earned about seven percent less than men on average. On Amazon's Mechanical Turk, where companies hire people for simple online tasks that are hard to automate, women earned about ten and a half percent less per hour. This was largely because they tended to take breaks between tasks, rather than working continuously, to handle caring responsibilities, particularly for young children. Many workers cite flexibility as a main reason for gig work, but that flexibility has limits, which may affect men and women differently. Surge pricing ties prices to demand, so it encourages workers to be online at busy times. But those times may clash with caring duties, creating a trade-off between flexibility and higher earnings.
key_points: Evidence on the gender pay gap in platform work is mixed, but many studies find women earn less than men, by a margin similar to the gap outside the gig economy.
One US analysis found female Uber drivers earned about 7 percent less than male drivers on average.
On Amazon's Mechanical Turk, women earned about 10.5 percent less per hour, largely because they took breaks between tasks to handle caregiving, especially for young children.

Flexibility, often cited as a main reason for gig work, has limits that may affect men and women differently, mainly because of surge pricing, which ties prices to demand and encourages working at busy times.
Those busy times can conflict with caregiving, creating a trade-off between flexibility and higher earnings.

items.script: Generally, biodiversity increases from the poles towards the tropics, so places at lower latitudes have more species than places at higher latitudes. This is known as the latitudinal gradient in species diversity. Several ecological factors may contribute to it, but the ultimate factor behind many of them is the higher average temperature at the equator compared with the poles. However, the pattern has exceptions. Although biodiversity on land declines from the equator to the poles, some studies claim this is unverified in aquatic ecosystems, especially marine ones. Parasites do not appear to follow the rule, and soil bacterial diversity is highest in temperate zones, which has been linked to carbon inputs and habitat connectivity.
