In twenty sixteen, an alternative explanation, the fractal biodiversity hypothesis, was proposed. It combines the size of the species pool with the fractal nature of ecosystems, and it uses three main variables: temperature, moisture and net primary production, which is how much new plant matter an ecosystem produces.
key_points: Biodiversity generally increases from the poles to the tropics, so lower latitudes have more species; this is the latitudinal gradient in species diversity.
Several ecological factors contribute, but the ultimate factor behind many of them is the higher mean temperature at the equator than at the poles.
The pattern holds on land, but some studies say it is unverified in aquatic, especially marine, ecosystems.
There are exceptions: parasites do not follow the rule, and soil bacterial diversity peaks in temperate zones, linked to carbon inputs and habitat connectivity.
In 2016, the fractal biodiversity hypothesis offered an alternative explanation, based on species pool size, the fractal nature of ecosystems, and temperature, moisture and net primary production.

items.topic: Long-term leakage of stored carbon dioxide
items.script: Will carbon dioxide stored deep underground stay there? Several trapping mechanisms hold it in place. An impermeable layer of rock called a caprock can trap it, and over a very long time it can also react with the rock to form carbonate minerals. The carbon dioxide tends to rise until it meets the caprock, then spreads sideways until it finds a gap. Faults near the injection zone could let it escape into the atmosphere, potentially endangering life nearby. Too much pressure could also fracture the rock and cause an earthquake, which research suggests would be too small to damage property but could cause a leak. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change says well-managed sites will likely retain over ninety-nine percent of the injected carbon dioxide for more than a thousand years. But these estimates rely on complex simulations, because field data is limited. And if very large amounts are stored, even a one percent leak over a thousand years could significantly affect the climate.
key_points: Carbon dioxide stored underground is held by several trapping mechanisms, including an impermeable caprock and extremely slow mineral trapping as it reacts with rock to form carbonates.
Injected carbon dioxide tends to rise until it meets the caprock, then spreads sideways until it finds a gap.

Faults near the injection zone could let it leak into the atmosphere, potentially endangering nearby life; excessive pressure could fracture rock and cause earthquakes that are too small to damage property but could cause leaks.
The IPCC says well-managed sites likely retain over 99 percent of injected carbon dioxide for more than a thousand years.
Leakage estimates rely on complex simulations because field data is limited, and with very large amounts stored, even 1 percent leakage over a thousand years could significantly affect the climate.

items.script: Soil erosion, especially from agriculture, is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution, because of the excess sediment flowing into the world's waterways. The sediment is a pollutant itself, and it also carries other pollutants, such as attached pesticides and heavy metals. For aquatic ecosystems, the effects can be catastrophic. Silt can smother the spawning beds of fish by filling the spaces between the gravel on the stream bed. It also reduces their food supply and causes serious breathing problems when it enters their gills. The diversity of aquatic plants and algae falls, and invertebrates cannot survive and reproduce. And although a sedimentation event may be short-lived, the ecological disruption from the mass die-off often lasts long into the future. Until erosion control measures were introduced in the nineteen eighties, one of the world's most serious long-running water erosion problems was in China, on the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers.
key_points: Soil erosion, especially from agriculture, is considered the leading global cause of diffuse water pollution because of excess sediment entering waterways.
Sediment is a pollutant itself and also carries attached pollutants such as pesticides and heavy metals.
Silt smothers fish spawning beds, reduces fish food supply and causes breathing problems in their gills; aquatic plant and algae diversity falls, and invertebrates cannot survive and reproduce.
A sedimentation event may be short-lived, but the disruption from the resulting mass die-off can last long into the future.
Until control measures in the 1980s, one of the world's most serious long-running water erosion problems was on China's Yellow and Yangtze Rivers.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Carlos
turns.text: I think tourism is good for cities. Tourists pay for hotels, meals and transport, so a lot of money comes into the local economy, and it creates jobs too. Look at Spain. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, mass tourism played a major role in its economic miracle.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Emma
turns.text: But local people often pay the price. In cities with heavy tourism, especially in the summer months, mass tourism has become a negative experience for residents. In July twenty twenty-four, thousands of people in Barcelona joined an anti-tourism protest as housing costs were rising.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Carlos
turns.text: I understand, but people also say travel broadens the mind. So tourism is good for visitors, not just for the economy.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Emma
turns.text: Maybe, but it can also sour relationships between hosts and guests. And it puts extra pressure on the local environment.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Yuki
turns.text: I can see both sides. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, scientists mostly talked about the harm tourism did to local communities. Since the nineteen eighties, they've recognised the positive side as well.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Emma
turns.text: So you think the good outweighs the bad?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Yuki
turns.text: Not exactly. Tourism depends on a place's culture and nature. World Heritage Sites, for example, are real tourist magnets. If tourism damages the environment, it damages the very thing that brings visitors. So I agree with Carlos about the income, but Emma is right that it needs to be managed.

key_points: Carlos (A) supports tourism: tourist spending brings income and jobs, as mass tourism did for Spain's economy in the 1960s and 1970s, and travel broadens the mind.
Emma (B) says mass tourism hurts residents, especially in summer (e.g. the 2024 Barcelona protest as housing costs rose), sours host-guest relations and puts pressure on the environment.
Yuki (C) sees both sides: early research (1960s-70s) stressed harm to host communities, and since the 1980s the benefits have been recognised too.

Yuki argues tourism depends on culture and nature (e.g. World Heritage Sites), so damaging the environment undermines tourism itself; she agrees with Carlos on the income and with Emma that tourism must be managed.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sam
turns.text: I think gig work is great, mainly because it's flexible. Eighty percent of women who work on DoorDash say flexibility is their main reason. You can even refuse an order. And it's easy to start, which helps young people who are still building their skills.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Nadia
turns.text: But look at what workers give up. Companies call them independent contractors, not employees, so they usually don't get overtime pay, paid sick days or health care from the company.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sam
turns.text: Some people really enjoy it. About one in five retired Americans do gig work, and almost all gig workers over sixty-five say they feel more fulfilled when they keep a job they enjoy.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Nadia
turns.text: Enjoy it? The apps put pressure on them through ratings. On platforms like Uber, a low rating from customers can mean less work or being removed completely. So workers, especially women, often put up with harassment just to protect their rating.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Leo
turns.text: The flexibility is real, but limited. With surge pricing, pay goes up when demand is high, so people must choose between flexibility and higher earnings. And many do it out of need. Seventy percent of new Uber drivers said rising living costs were their main reason for joining.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sam
turns.text: So what's your answer?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Leo
turns.text: Gig work is unlikely to disappear, so let's make it fairer. Since January twenty twenty-five, Singapore has given gig workers injury insurance and the right to bargain together. That keeps the flexibility and adds protection.

key_points: Sam (A) values gig work's flexibility (the main reason for 80% of women on DoorDash), the right to refuse orders and easy entry for young people; about one in five retired Americans do gig work, and almost all gig workers over 65 say keeping a job they enjoy makes them feel more fulfilled.

Nadia (B) says workers lose out: as independent contractors they usually get no overtime, sick pay or company health care, and customer ratings pressure them (especially women) into tolerating harassment.
Leo (C) says the flexibility is real but limited: surge pricing forces a trade-off between flexibility and earnings, and many work out of need (70% of new Uber drivers cited rising living costs).

Leo takes a middle position: gig work will not disappear, so it should be made fairer, as Singapore did from 2025 with injury insurance and collective bargaining, keeping flexibility while adding protection.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Ravi
turns.text: I think city life is better. Cities offer more jobs, better education and specialist services. Some older people even move to cities to be near doctors and hospitals. And people in cities are more productive than people in the countryside.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Grace
turns.text: But city life has a cost. Living costs are higher, and many people feel stressed and isolated. A big study in Sweden found that people who live in cities have a twenty percent higher chance of developing depression.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Ravi
turns.text: Maybe, but city people are more active. In the United States, people in rural areas exercise less and have higher rates of obesity.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Grace
turns.text: That doesn't help poor migrants. In many cases, they come from the countryside for work, but they can't find a job or pay for a house, so they end up in slums.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Omar
turns.text: You're both partly right. On average, health is better in cities than in rural areas, but people in slums suffer much more from disease and early death. So the real question is how cities are planned.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Grace
turns.text: Planned in what way?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Omar
turns.text: Walkable neighbourhoods, with homes, shops and offices mixed together, and affordable housing. Walkable communities have a thirty-eight percent higher economic output per person than less walkable cities. And United Nations agencies prefer infrastructure to be in place before a city grows, not after.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Grace
turns.text: I still prefer the countryside, but good planning would help.

key_points: Ravi (A) prefers cities: more jobs, better education and specialist services such as doctors and hospitals, higher productivity, and (in the US) more physical activity than in rural areas.
Grace (B) stresses the costs: higher living costs, stress and isolation, a 20% higher chance of depression (Swedish study), and poor migrants who cannot find work or housing ending up in slums.
Omar (C) says both are partly right: health is better in cities on average, but slum dwellers suffer far more disease and early death, so planning is the real issue.

Omar recommends walkable, mixed-use neighbourhoods with affordable housing (38% higher economic output per person) and building infrastructure before cities grow; Grace still prefers the countryside but agrees planning would help.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Anna
turns.text: I think our city should spend much more on buses and trains. Public transport is better for the environment. One American study found it uses about half the fuel that cars do, and subways can cut a city's carbon dioxide emissions by around half.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Tom
turns.text: But subways are very expensive. Building one costs about two hundred million dollars per kilometre. And one study found that better access to public transport made no real difference to the number of cars in the long term.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Anna
turns.text: Maybe, but it's also much safer. People in communities built around public transport have about one fifth of the crash injuries and deaths of car-based communities.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Tom
turns.text: Safer on the roads, perhaps, but a Dutch study found higher crime rates on public transport than in cars.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Mei
turns.text: What matters most to me is who uses it. Children, older people without cars, people without a driving licence and wheelchair users all rely on it. In poorer areas, it gives people transport they couldn't otherwise afford.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Tom
turns.text: I agree, but is it worth the money everywhere?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Mei
turns.text: Not everywhere, and there I partly agree with you. People use it daily in dense areas where homes, shops and jobs are mixed, but only now and then in spread-out suburbs. So we should build it together with better city planning.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Anna
turns.text: Fine, but I still think we should start investing now.

key_points: Anna (A) wants much more investment: public transport uses about half the fuel of cars, subways can roughly halve a city's carbon dioxide emissions, and transit-based communities have about one fifth of the crash casualties.

Tom (B) doubts the value: subways cost about 200 million dollars per kilometre, better access did not reduce car numbers in the long term, and a Dutch study found more crime on public transport than in cars.
Mei (C) stresses who it serves: children, older people without cars, people without a licence, wheelchair users, and people in poorer areas who could not otherwise afford transport.
Mei partly agrees with Tom: it is used daily in dense, mixed-use areas but only occasionally in sprawl, so it should be built with better planning; Anna still wants to invest now.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sofia
turns.text: I think museums should give back objects taken from other countries. Take the Moai, the stone figures from Easter Island. Since eighteen sixty-eight, several have been taken to big Western museums. The islanders want them back, because they see them as ancestors and family.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Daniel
turns.text: I understand, but it isn't always simple. In the United States, a law requires museums to return Native American remains, but they face problems like incomplete records and limited resources. Sometimes it's hard even to know which community the remains belong to.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sofia
turns.text: Hard, but not impossible. Greece has asked again and again for the Parthenon marbles, which Lord Elgin took in eighteen oh five. And a twenty eighteen report in France looked at African countries' claims to objects taken illegally.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Daniel
turns.text: Some museums also say keeping human remains has scientific value. And Europe has a patchwork of national laws. In Germany and France, requests are judged case by case.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Amira
turns.text: For me, giving things back is only part of it. People in the decolonization movement say museums are just a box of things. They show one-sided stories and leave out other points of view.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Daniel
turns.text: So what would you change?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Amira
turns.text: Museums should tell the stories of groups that are often ignored, like the Black Miners Museum in Nottingham. But like Sofia, I think change is coming. There's growing pressure from the public and governments for museums to face their colonial past.

key_points: Sofia (A) wants museums to return objects taken from other countries, e.g. the Moai (seen by Easter Islanders as ancestors and family), the Parthenon marbles Greece keeps requesting, and African objects taken illegally (2018 French report).

Daniel (B) says returning is not simple: under a US law museums must return Native American remains but face incomplete records, limited resources and unclear community links; some museums claim scientific value, and European laws vary, with case-by-case decisions.

Amira (C) says returning objects is only part of it: decolonization supporters call museums 'a box of things' with one-sided stories, so museums should also tell the stories of ignored groups (e.g. the Black Miners Museum in Nottingham).

Amira, like Sofia, expects change: there is growing pressure from the public and governments for museums to face their colonial past; Daniel stresses practical difficulties rather than rejecting returns.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Lucas
turns.text: I think hydroelectric dams are one of the best sources of clean electricity. They burn no fuel, so generating power produces no carbon dioxide, and hydro has one of the lowest lifecycle emissions of any source. Reservoirs can also supply water for farming and control floods.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Hana
turns.text: But think about what's lost. Large reservoirs flood huge areas, sometimes destroying forests, marshland and grassland, and often force people and wildlife to move. In two thousand, the World Commission on Dams estimated that dams had displaced forty to eighty million people.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Lucas
turns.text: That's a real cost, but compare it with coal. Hydro produces no sulfur dioxide or nitrogen oxides, and it avoids the dangers of coal mining and the health effects of coal pollution.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Hana
turns.text: It still harms rivers. Turbines kill fish, for example seventy percent of the eels that pass through die immediately. And dam failures can be catastrophic. When the Banqiao Dam in China failed in nineteen seventy-five, the flood killed twenty-six thousand people.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Kofi
turns.text: You're both right, but it depends on location. In tropical rainforest, flooded plants rot and release methane. If the reservoir is large for its power output and the forest wasn't cleared, it may emit more greenhouse gas than an oil-fired plant. In Canada and northern Europe, emissions are typically two to eight percent of a fossil fuel plant's.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Lucas
turns.text: So location matters. Anything else?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Kofi
turns.text: Climate change. One study of the Colorado River suggests that a two degree rise in temperature, with ten percent less precipitation, might cut river run-off by up to forty percent. That's why the International Energy Agency has called for strong sustainability standards for all hydropower.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Hana
turns.text: Standards would help, but I'd still build fewer large dams.

key_points: Lucas (A) supports dams: no fuel and no carbon dioxide during generation, very low lifecycle emissions, irrigation and flood control, and none of coal's air pollution or mining hazards.

Hana (B) opposes large dams: reservoirs flood forests and grassland and displace people and wildlife (40-80 million people by 2000), turbines kill fish (70% of eels), and failures can be catastrophic (Banqiao, 1975).

Kofi (C) says it depends on location: tropical reservoirs over uncleared forest may emit more greenhouse gas than an oil-fired plant, while those in Canada and northern Europe emit only 2-8% of a fossil plant's.

Kofi adds that climate change may sharply cut river flow (Colorado study, up to 40%) and backs the IEA's call for strong sustainability standards; Lucas accepts location matters, Hana still wants fewer large dams.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Mark
turns.text: I think obesity mostly comes down to personal choices. The basic cause is that people consume more calories than their bodies use. Long-term changes that cut calories or increase exercise tend to produce some lasting weight loss, and sticking to a diet matters more than which diet you choose.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Aisha
turns.text: If it were that simple, it would work for more people. Only between two and twenty percent of people who change their lifestyle manage to keep the weight off in the long term. And genes alone can't explain why obesity has risen so dramatically. So we have to look at society, not just individuals.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Mark
turns.text: What in society, exactly?

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Aisha
turns.text: Food prices, for a start. In the United States, farm subsidies have made the main ingredients of processed food cheap compared with fruit and vegetables. Neighbourhood design matters too. In one American study, people in the most walkable areas were two point four times more likely to get enough exercise than people in the least walkable areas.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Lena
turns.text: I'd add biology. According to the Endocrine Society, obesity isn't just about extra calories. The body also adapts to a heavier weight as its new normal, which helps explain why effective treatments have been hard to find. So blaming individuals is unfair, and it has a cost. People with obesity face stereotypes and bullying, and they're paid less for the same job, about six percent less for women and three percent less for men.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Mark
turns.text: Discrimination is wrong, of course. But we can't ignore the health risks. On average, obesity reduces life expectancy by six to seven years.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Lena
turns.text: I'm not denying that. The fat acceptance movement mainly wants to reduce discrimination, although some members also question the link between obesity and poor health, and I wouldn't go that far. We can take the risks seriously and still treat people fairly.

key_points: Mark (A) sees obesity as mainly personal choice: people consume more calories than they use; long-term diet and exercise changes bring some lasting weight loss, and sticking to a diet matters more than its type.

Aisha (B) blames the environment: only 2-20% keep weight off long term, genes cannot explain the dramatic rise, US farm subsidies make processed food cheap compared with fruit and vegetables, and walkable areas make enough exercise 2.4 times more likely.

Lena (C) adds a biological view: the body adapts to a heavier weight as its new normal (Endocrine Society), so blaming individuals is unfair and causes stigma: stereotypes, bullying and lower pay for the same job (about 6% less for women, 3% for men).

Mark agrees discrimination is wrong but stresses the health risk (six to seven years' lower life expectancy on average); Lena accepts the risks, supports reducing discrimination but not questioning the health link, and wants fair treatment.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Ben
turns.text: I think recycling is clearly worth it, mainly because it saves so much energy. Recycling aluminium cans saves ninety-five percent of the energy needed to make new aluminium, and a paper mill uses forty percent less energy when it starts from recycled paper.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Clara
turns.text: Energy is one thing, but money is another. Generally, it's more expensive for cities to recycle household waste than to send it to a landfill. One critic says it can cost a city more than twice as much. And collecting recyclables often needs a second truck.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Ben
turns.text: But cities have saved money too. New York once called recycling a drain on the city, and two years later its leaders realised an efficient system could save over twenty million dollars. And a Danish study found recycling was the most efficient way to deal with household waste in eighty-three percent of cases.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Clara
turns.text: Look at plastic, though. New plastic resin costs forty percent less than recycled resin, and in the United States only around six or seven percent of plastic is recycled at all.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Hiro
turns.text: I think you're comparing the wrong prices. Market prices ignore pollution. Making new plastic may cause more pollution than recycling it, but that cost isn't counted. A life cycle assessment, or a carbon tax, would show the true cost.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Clara
turns.text: And what about the extra truck?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Hiro
turns.text: Supporters point out that recycling paper removes the need for a logging truck, so the energy balances out. And communities save money when recycling replaces their normal waste collection instead of being added on top. The bigger problem is that most products aren't designed to be recycled in the first place.

key_points: Ben (A) says recycling is worth it: large energy savings (95% for aluminium cans, 40% for paper), New York found an efficient system could save over 20 million dollars, and a Danish study found it the most efficient option in 83% of cases.

Clara (B) says it generally costs cities more than landfill (sometimes over twice as much), often needs a second truck, new plastic resin is 40% cheaper than recycled, and only 6-7% of US plastic is recycled.
Hiro (C) says market prices mislead because they ignore the pollution from making new materials; a life cycle assessment or a carbon tax would show the true cost.

Hiro answers Clara's points (recycling paper saves a logging truck; cities save money when recycling replaces rather than adds to normal collection) and says the bigger problem is that products are not designed for recycling.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Pedro
turns.text: Farmers use antibiotics for good reasons. With the world's population growing, there's constant pressure to produce more meat. Antibiotics in feed are used to help animals grow and to prevent infections, and they do give better yields. Besides, the evidence linking farm use to resistance is limited.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Ingrid
turns.text: Limited evidence isn't the same as no risk. In the United States, about eighty percent of all antibiotic use is in agriculture, and around seventy percent of those drugs are medically important. Resistant bacteria can pass into the food we eat, with potentially fatal results. That's why a World Health Organization advisory group said medically important antibiotics should be banned for both growth promotion and disease prevention in farm animals.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Pedro
turns.text: My worry is that a complete ban would hurt farmers.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Rahul
turns.text: Europe suggests that worry may be overstated. By two thousand four, several European countries had reduced resistance in humans by limiting antibiotics in farming, without harming animal health or raising costs. Then in two thousand six, the European Union banned antibiotics for growth promotion, and in Scandinavia there's evidence the ban lowered resistance in animal bacteria.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Ingrid
turns.text: So a ban works.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Rahul
turns.text: It can, but one region acting alone isn't enough. Forty countries still use antibiotics to promote growth, and worldwide, antibiotic use in livestock is predicted to rise by sixty-seven percent by twenty thirty. I'd also put vets in control, as in the United States, where since twenty seventeen, medically important antibiotics in animal feed or water need a veterinary order or prescription.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Pedro
turns.text: Vets deciding case by case, I could live with that.

key_points: Pedro (A) defends farm antibiotics: they are used to boost growth and prevent infections and give better yields amid pressure to produce more meat, and evidence linking farm use to resistance is limited.

Ingrid (B) wants a ban: about 80% of US antibiotic use is agricultural (about 70% of it medically important), resistant bacteria can reach people through food, and a WHO advisory group said these drugs should be prohibited for growth promotion and disease prevention.

Rahul (C) questions Pedro's fear for farmers: several European countries cut human resistance by limiting farm use without harming animal health or costs, and after the EU's 2006 ban on growth promoters there is evidence of lower resistance in Scandinavian animal bacteria.

Rahul agrees with Ingrid that bans can work but says action must be global (40 countries still use growth promoters; worldwide livestock use predicted to rise 67% by 2030) and wants vets in control, as in the US since 2017; Pedro accepts vet oversight.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Elena
turns.text: I think we should build large solar farms as fast as possible. Over their life cycle, solar farms emit less than fifty grams of greenhouse gases per kilowatt hour, compared with about five hundred for gas and a thousand for coal. Making panels causes some pollution, but after a carbon payback time of several years, they provide clean energy for the rest of their thirty-year life.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Jack
turns.text: Emissions are low, but land is the problem. One study found that if Japan and South Korea got a large share of their electricity from solar farms by twenty fifty, panels could cover up to about five percent of their land. That could mean losing forests and farmland, and local residents may oppose it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Elena
turns.text: But worldwide, the land used for solar has minimal ecological impact.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Jack
turns.text: Worldwide, maybe, but not locally. Solar panels can raise the local temperature, and in large desert installations, the effect can be stronger than an urban heat island.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Priya
turns.text: I think the land problem can be reduced. Japan and South Korea already farm under solar panels or use floating solar. Grasses and flowers can be planted between panels to support pollinators. And if panels go on buildings and other built-up areas, solar's land use can drop to the level of gas power.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Jack
turns.text: Rooftops I can support. But aren't materials a problem too?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Priya
turns.text: Yes. The International Energy Agency expects demand for copper to double by twenty forty, so recycling and reuse matter. Old panels are sometimes reused in developing countries, and some academics want panels designed to be easier to repair.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Elena
turns.text: Fine, but none of that is a reason to slow down.

key_points: Elena (A) wants large solar farms built fast: life-cycle emissions under 50 grams per kilowatt hour versus about 500 for gas and 1,000 for coal, clean power for the rest of a 30-year life after a carbon payback of several years, and minimal ecological impact of land use worldwide.

Jack (B) worries about land and local effects: panels could cover up to about 5% of land in Japan and South Korea by 2050, threatening forests and farmland and causing local opposition, and panels can raise local temperatures (in deserts more than an urban heat island).
Priya (C) says the land problem can be reduced: farming under panels, floating solar, pollinator plants between panels, and panels on buildings, which cut land use to the level of gas.
Priya also warns of material limits (copper demand doubling by 2040) and supports recycling, reuse and repairable panels; Jack supports rooftops, while Elena refuses to slow down.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Rachel
turns.text: I think we're too quick to condemn placebos in everyday medicine. In one Israeli study, sixty percent of the physicians and head nurses surveyed said they had used placebos, and only five percent thought they should be strictly prohibited. Some also argue that blanket consent, where patients agree in advance to unspecified treatment, makes the practice ethical.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: David
turns.text: Common practice isn't the same as good practice. A placebo disguised as real medication is deceptive, and it could harm the relationship between doctor and patient in the long run. On the grounds of patient autonomy, some argue that people should always be told the name of the drug, its side effects and the other treatment options.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Rachel
turns.text: But we shouldn't dismiss the patients who respond. As an editorial in the British Medical Journal pointed out, getting pain relief from a placebo doesn't mean the pain isn't real.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: David
turns.text: I agree, and the same editorial said that using placebos to test whether pain is real is misguided. But that doesn't justify prescribing them. Doctors and pharmacists could face charges of fraud or malpractice, and a placebo might delay the proper diagnosis of a serious condition. A committee of the British House of Commons also warned that the placebo effect is unreliable and unpredictable.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Tomasz
turns.text: I'd take a middle path, and doctors themselves seem divided. In a survey of more than ten thousand American physicians, twenty-four percent would prescribe a placebo simply because a patient wanted treatment, fifty-eight percent would not, and for the rest it depended on the circumstances.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Rachel
turns.text: So what's your middle path?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Tomasz
turns.text: Use the effect without the deception. Ben Goldacre argues that doctors should use the placebo effect to enhance medicines that actually work, and Edzard Ernst says a good doctor should be able to pass on a placebo effect through the compassion they show. What worries me more is alternative medicine. The placebo researcher Fabrizio Benedetti warns of a growing industry that preys on the vulnerable.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: David
turns.text: On that last point, I completely agree.

key_points: Rachel (A) defends placebo use in everyday medicine: it is common (60% of surveyed Israeli physicians and head nurses; only 5% want a strict ban), blanket consent may make it ethical, and placebo pain relief does not mean the pain is unreal.

David (B) opposes disguised placebos: they are deceptive, may harm the doctor-patient relationship and patient autonomy, risk fraud or malpractice charges, may delay diagnosis of serious conditions, and the effect is unreliable and unpredictable (UK House of Commons committee).
David accepts the point about real pain but notes the same editorial called using placebos to test pain misguided, which does not justify prescribing them.

Tomasz (C) takes a middle path: doctors are divided (US survey: 24% would, 58% would not, the rest it depends), so the placebo effect should be used without deception, by enhancing effective medicines (Goldacre) and through compassion (Ernst).
Tomasz and David agree in worrying about alternative medicine preying on the vulnerable (Benedetti).

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Julia
turns.text: I think nudges are one of the smartest tools a government has. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein defined a nudge as any feature of the way choices are presented that changes behaviour predictably, without banning options or significantly changing economic incentives. Putting fruit at eye level counts as a nudge. Banning junk food doesn't. Britain set up a Behavioural Insights Team, often called the Nudge Unit, in twenty ten.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Marcus
turns.text: That definition sounds harmless, but critics call nudges manipulative, and some say nudging is just a polite word for psychological manipulation. Others have charged that nudges reduce autonomy and threaten dignity. And the techniques are getting subtler. One recent study suggests that small phone vibrations can increase purchasing without people being consciously aware of it, and it asks whether that blurs the line between persuasion and coercion.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Julia
turns.text: But a real nudge must be easy and cheap to avoid, so no one is forced into anything. Sunstein has answered these charges at length in his book The Ethics of Influence. And the same authors introduced the idea of sludge, meaning confusing forms or hidden fees that make it harder to do something beneficial. Removing sludge is hardly manipulation.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Aiko
turns.text: My concern is less about ethics and more about evidence. Behavioural economics has a replication problem. Many studies fail when they're repeated, and a twenty twenty-four review in the Wall Street Journal reported that fewer than half of nudging experiments kept their long-term impact when they were re-tested. Even scholars in the field admit that small effect sizes and limited sample diversity make results hard to generalise.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Marcus
turns.text: So nudges may be manipulative and not even work.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Aiko
turns.text: That's not quite what I'm saying. They just can't be the whole answer. Much of the research relies on people from Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic societies. In poorer countries, reminders and nudges often aren't enough to change health behaviour, and extra measures like financial incentives or subsidised transport are frequently needed.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Julia
turns.text: That's fair. I'd still use nudges, but test them properly where they'll actually be used.

key_points: Julia (A) supports nudges as defined by Thaler and Sunstein: they change behaviour predictably without banning options or changing incentives (fruit at eye level, not junk-food bans); Britain set up a 'Nudge Unit' in 2010.

Marcus (B) raises ethical objections: critics call nudging manipulation that reduces autonomy and threatens dignity, and subtle tactics such as phone vibrations may increase buying without conscious awareness, raising the question of whether they blur persuasion and coercion.
Julia replies that real nudges must be easy and cheap to avoid, Sunstein has defended them at length, and removing 'sludge' such as confusing forms or hidden fees is not manipulation.

Aiko (C) questions the evidence rather than the ethics: many studies fail to replicate, a 2024 Wall Street Journal review found fewer than half of nudging experiments kept long-term effects, effects are small and samples narrow (mostly Western, educated, rich societies), and in poorer countries nudges often need financial incentives or subsidised transport.
Aiko rejects Marcus's conclusion that nudges simply do not work, saying only that they cannot be the whole answer; Julia agrees to keep using nudges but test them where they will be used.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sarah
turns.text: I find the evidence alarming. Stanford Medicine reports that microplastics are invariably found in the human body, even in babies, through the placenta and breast milk, and in the brain and heart. A twenty twenty-four study found that patients with microplastics in their arterial plaque had a higher risk of heart attack, stroke and death.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Victor
turns.text: Being in the body isn't the same as causing harm. The health effects are still being tested, and although microplastics have been associated with problems like respiratory disease, we don't know if they're the cause. Several high-profile studies have been contested. Fat in human tissue can be mistaken for plastic, and coatings from laboratory gloves can rub off and cause errors.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sarah
turns.text: Even so, the authors of one of those studies say even a smaller amount of plastic in human tissue would be unacceptable. There should be none, they say. And microplastics often contain additives like bisphenol A and phthalates, which are known to disrupt hormones.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Victor
turns.text: That's a value judgement, not proof of harm. When mice were fed a mixture of microplastics, researchers saw no obvious severe toxicity in organs such as the liver, heart and kidneys. And detection methods still aren't fully standardised, so results can vary a lot between laboratories.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Nia
turns.text: I think you're both missing the point. Whatever the health verdict, we should focus on prevention that works. Treatment plants capture microplastics from wastewater, for example, but they end up in sludge that's often spread on farms as fertiliser, so the plastic washes into waterways anyway.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Sarah
turns.text: What about cleaning up the oceans?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Nia
turns.text: The Ocean Cleanup, run by a Dutch foundation, has been dismissed by almost all microplastics experts. It only targets pieces larger than two centimetres, in the top three metres of water, while most plastic circulates much deeper. I'd rather have laws with real penalties, like England's microbead ban, which comes with fines. Japan's law specifies no penalties at all.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Victor
turns.text: On prevention, I agree. It makes sense even while the evidence is uncertain.

key_points: Sarah (A) is alarmed: microplastics are found throughout the body, even in babies (placenta, breast milk), the brain and the heart; a 2024 study linked microplastics in arterial plaque to higher risk of heart attack, stroke and death; additives such as bisphenol A and phthalates disrupt hormones.

Victor (B) says harm is not proven: health effects are still being tested, links with disease may not be causal, some high-profile studies are contested (fat mistaken for plastic, glove contamination), mice showed no obvious severe organ toxicity, and detection methods are not standardised.
Sarah counters that a contested study's authors say even smaller amounts in tissue would be unacceptable ('there should be none'); Victor calls this a value judgement, not proof.

Nia (C) wants the focus on effective prevention: treatment-plant sludge spread on farms returns microplastics to waterways, experts dismiss The Ocean Cleanup (only large pieces near the surface), and laws need real penalties (England's microbead ban with fines vs Japan's law with none).
Victor agrees with Nia that prevention makes sense even while the health evidence is uncertain.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Mateo
turns.text: I'm convinced that being bilingual is good for the brain. Studies in the early nineteen nineties confirmed that students who complete bilingual instruction perform better academically and show more cognitive flexibility, including a better ability to analyse abstract visual patterns. Bilinguals also generally do better on auditory tasks, like detecting gaps in sounds or recognising pitch patterns.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Helen
turns.text: I'd be careful. There's no evidence for a bilingual advantage in executive function. Claims that highly proficient bilinguals have better executive function and a later onset of dementia have come under strong criticism, because the results keep failing to replicate. Even the idea that bilinguals are better at learning languages persisted partly because of publication bias, and current meta-analyses find no effect.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Mateo
turns.text: Then look at the real world. A Swiss study linked multilingualism to higher salaries and more productive firms, and its authors say it adds ten percent to Switzerland's gross domestic product. In the United States, bilingual people were found to earn around three thousand dollars a year more.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Helen
turns.text: I don't doubt the economic benefits. Bilinguals can do things monolinguals can't, such as serving customers who only speak a minority language. But that's a practical skill, not a sharper mind.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Kenji
turns.text: I think the real problem is measurement. Many earlier studies didn't reliably measure the bilinguals they tested. Even Mateo's auditory studies found that a person's level of proficiency in the second language made a difference. An emerging view is that researchers need validated, detailed measures of language experience to identify the conditions under which any cognitive effects appear.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Mateo
turns.text: So the advantages might be real, but only for some people?

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Kenji
turns.text: Possibly, but we can't say until the measurement improves. The same goes for claims that people's personality changes when they switch languages. There's been little rigorous research on that, and François Grosjean suggests it's most probably a shift in behaviour to fit the situation.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Helen
turns.text: That I agree with. Better measurement first, bold claims later.

key_points: Mateo (A) believes bilingualism benefits the mind: early-1990s studies found students completing bilingual instruction did better academically with more cognitive flexibility, and bilinguals show better auditory processing; he also cites economic gains (10% of Swiss GDP, about 3,000 dollars a year more in the US).

Helen (B) is sceptical of cognitive claims: there is no evidence of an executive-function advantage, claims about better executive function and later dementia keep failing to replicate, and the idea that bilinguals learn languages more easily persisted partly through publication bias, with meta-analyses finding no effect.
Helen accepts the economic benefits (e.g. serving minority-language customers) but calls them a practical skill, not a sharper mind.

Kenji (C) says the core problem is measurement: earlier studies did not reliably measure their bilingual samples and proficiency matters, so validated, detailed measures of language experience are needed to find when effects appear; he applies the same caution to claims of personality change (little rigorous research; Grosjean: a behaviour shift to fit the situation).
Helen agrees with Kenji; Mateo accepts the advantages may apply only to some people.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Olivia
turns.text: I think we need a much bigger commitment to carbon capture and storage. In twenty twenty-three, it captured only about zero point one percent of global emissions, yet climate models show it capturing about a billion tonnes by twenty thirty. The International Energy Agency is calling for more commitment. It can also preserve jobs in regions that rely on emissions-intensive industry.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Kwame
turns.text: That's exactly what worries me. Fossil fuel companies promote carbon capture heavily, suggesting it will let the fossil fuel era be extended. At the twenty twenty-three United Nations climate conference, at least four hundred and seventy-five carbon capture lobbyists were given access. Many environmental groups see it as an unproven, expensive distraction that keeps us dependent on fossil fuels.

turns.speaker: A
turns.name: Olivia
turns.text: But slow progress is a reason to invest more, not less.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Kwame
turns.text: Or it's a sign the concept is unlikely to succeed, as some observers conclude. And think about who lives nearby. In the United States, plants that could be fitted with capture are disproportionately in poor or minority communities, and local groups often prefer to see them shut down, with the money going into cleaner production such as renewable electricity.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Elif
turns.text: I think we should judge each project by what it actually achieves. Most studies assume power plants capture eighty-five to ninety percent of their carbon dioxide, but industry representatives say real rates are closer to seventy-five. And at the Petra Nova coal plant, one study found the actual emissions cut would average only ten point eight percent over twenty years.

turns.speaker: B
turns.name: Kwame
turns.text: Which proves my point.

turns.speaker: C
turns.name: Elif
turns.text: Partly. It shows that accounting matters. When captured carbon is used to pump out more oil, scientific papers are roughly evenly split on whether that raises or lowers emissions. Definitions matter too. The twenty twenty-three agreement to phase down unabated coal never defined the term, so a plant capturing only thirty percent could count as abated. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change talks about ninety percent or more for power plants. With clear standards, I'd support it where it genuinely works.

key_points: Olivia (A) wants a much bigger commitment: carbon capture handled only about 0.1% of global emissions in 2023 while climate models show about a billion tonnes by 2030, the IEA calls for more commitment, and it can preserve jobs in regions with emissions-intensive industry.

Kwame (B) opposes it: fossil fuel companies promote it to extend the fossil fuel era (at least 475 lobbyists at the 2023 UN conference), environmental groups see it as an unproven, expensive distraction, and nearby poor or minority communities often prefer closure and investment in renewables.
Olivia and Kwame disagree about slow progress: for her a reason to invest more, for him a sign the concept is unlikely to succeed.

Elif (C) wants each project judged on real results and honest accounting: capture may be about 75% rather than the assumed 85-90%, Petra Nova's cut may average only 10.8% over 20 years, and studies are evenly split on capture used for oil recovery.

Elif partly agrees with Kwame but would support carbon capture under clear standards, since 'unabated' was left undefined in the 2023 agreement (30% capture could count) while the IPCC refers to 90% or more for power plants.

items.situation: Your new neighbour has played loud music until after midnight every night this week. You start work very early, so you are getting very little sleep. This morning you meet your neighbour at the front door of your building, and they greet you in a friendly way. What would you say to your neighbour?
key_points: Goal: politely ask the neighbour to keep the music down late at night.
Greets the neighbour in a friendly way before raising the problem.
Explains the problem: loud music after midnight all week, and you start work very early.
Suggests a reasonable solution, such as turning the music down after a certain time.
Keeps a friendly, non-accusing tone suitable for a neighbour.

items.situation: Last week you bought a pair of running shoes as a birthday present for your brother, but they are too small for him. He has not worn them, and you still have the receipt. You go back to the shop, and an assistant asks how she can help you. What would you say to the shop assistant?
key_points: Goal: ask to exchange the shoes for a larger size, or for a refund.
Explains that the shoes were a birthday present bought last week and are too small.
Mentions that the shoes have not been worn and that you have the receipt.
Asks about the options politely, with requests such as 'Could I...' or 'Would it be possible...'.

items.topic: Declining to look after a dog
items.situation: Your friend is going on holiday next week and asks you to look after her dog at your flat. You would like to help, but pets are not allowed in your building, and you work long hours. Your friend is waiting for your answer. What would you say to your friend?
key_points: Goal: kindly say no to looking after the dog while keeping the friendship.
Shows that you would like to help and apologises for saying no.
Explains both reasons: pets are not allowed in your building and you work long hours.
Suggests an alternative, such as a pet sitter, another friend, or visiting the dog at her home when you can.
Uses a warm, friendly tone.

items.situation: Your friend lent you her camera for your holiday. On the last day, you dropped it, and now the screen is cracked, although the camera still takes photos. Today your friend calls you and asks when she can have it back. What would you say to your friend?
key_points: Goal: tell the friend honestly that the camera is damaged and take responsibility.
Apologises sincerely.
Explains what happened: you dropped it on the last day and the screen cracked, but it still takes photos.
Offers to pay for the repair and agrees when to return the camera.
Keeps an honest, apologetic and friendly tone.

items.situation: You ordered a vegetarian pizza for delivery and paid for it online. When the driver hands it to you and you open the box, you see that it has meat on it, and you do not eat meat. The driver is still at your door. What would you say to the driver?
key_points: Goal: explain that the order is wrong and get a vegetarian replacement or a refund.
Explains that you ordered a vegetarian pizza, but this one has meat, which you do not eat.
Mentions that you have already paid online.
Asks what can be done, for example whether the driver can contact the restaurant.
Stays calm and polite, without blaming the driver personally.

items.situation: Your essay is due in two days, but you have been ill with a high fever for most of this week, and you have a note from your doctor. You have finished only about half of the essay. You see your tutor in the corridor after class. What would you say to your tutor?
key_points: Goal: politely ask the tutor for a short extension on the essay.
Explains the reason: a high fever for most of the week, so only about half the essay is done.
Mentions the doctor's note and offers to show it or follow the official process.
Proposes a specific, realistic new deadline.
Uses a respectful, formal register suitable for a tutor.

items.situation: You are working on a group presentation with three classmates. One member has missed the last two meetings and has not replied to the group messages, and the presentation is next week. Today you meet him by chance in the library. What would you say to your classmate?
key_points: Goal: get the classmate involved again and agree on his part before next week's presentation.
Starts in a friendly way and asks if everything is all right, instead of accusing him.
Explains the problem: he missed two meetings, has not replied to messages, and the group needs his input.
Proposes a concrete next step, such as a specific task, a deadline, or the next meeting time.
Keeps a cooperative, supportive tone.

items.situation: You need a particular book for an assignment that is due in ten days, but the only copy in the library has been borrowed by someone else and is not due back for three weeks. You go to the help desk to speak to the librarian. What would you say to the librarian?
key_points: Goal: find a way to get the book, or a suitable alternative, before the assignment is due.
Explains the timing problem: the only copy is on loan for three weeks, but the assignment is due in ten days.
Asks about specific options, such as reserving or recalling the book, an electronic version, or a copy from another library.
Uses polite requests and thanks the librarian.

items.situation: You live in university accommodation. The heating in your room has not worked for five days, and the nights are getting very cold. You reported the problem by email on Monday, but nobody has replied or come to fix it. You now visit the accommodation office in person. What would you say to the staff member there?
key_points: Goal: get the heating repaired as soon as possible.
Explains the problem: no heating for five days while the nights are very cold.
Mentions the email report on Monday that got no reply and no repair.
Asks for a specific action, such as a repair date or a temporary heater until it is fixed.
Stays firm but polite, without blaming the staff member personally.

items.situation: A classmate you get on well with asks to see your finished assignment so that he can copy some of your answers. The assignment is individual work, and copying would break the university rules. You want to stay on good terms with him. What would you say to your classmate?
key_points: Goal: refuse to share the assignment while staying on good terms.
Says no clearly but kindly, showing understanding that he may be under pressure.
Explains the reason: it is individual work and copying breaks the university rules, which puts you both at risk.
Offers other help, such as explaining difficult parts, studying together, or suggesting he ask the tutor.
Uses a friendly, non-judgemental tone.

items.situation: You work for a company that supplies office furniture. An important client's order should have arrived last Monday, but a problem at your warehouse has delayed it, and it will now arrive on Friday. The client phones you and is clearly annoyed about the delay. What would you say to the client?
key_points: Goal: apologise for the late delivery and keep the client's trust.
Acknowledges the client's frustration and apologises sincerely, without making excuses.
Explains briefly that a warehouse problem caused the delay and confirms delivery on Friday.
Offers reassurance or a gesture, such as delivery updates, a discount or free delivery.
Uses a calm, professional and formal register.

items.situation: Your manager asks you to lead a new project that starts next week. You find the project interesting, but you are already working on two other projects with deadlines at the end of this month, and taking on more now could lower the quality of your work. What would you say to your manager?
key_points: Goal: politely decline leading the project now while keeping a good relationship with the manager.
Thanks the manager and shows genuine interest in the project.
Explains the reason: two current projects due at the end of the month, and a risk to the quality of your work.
Proposes an alternative, such as joining after the current deadlines, taking a smaller role, or agreeing priorities together.
Uses a respectful, professional register.

items.situation: You booked a meeting room at a hotel for an important meeting with clients. When you arrive, the projector does not work, and the room has not been set up in the way you requested. Your clients will arrive in thirty minutes. You ask to speak to the hotel manager. What would you say to the manager?
key_points: Goal: complain clearly and get the room ready before the clients arrive.
Describes the specific problems: the projector does not work and the room is not set up as requested.
Stresses the urgency: the clients arrive in thirty minutes.
Asks for concrete action, such as a working projector, another room, or staff to set it up now, and may raise compensation later.
Stays firm but professional and polite.

items.situation: You are responsible for purchasing at a small company. Your main supplier has just told you that their prices will rise next month. You want to keep working with them, but your budget is tight. Your company has been a loyal customer for several years and regularly places large orders. What would you say to the supplier?
key_points: Goal: negotiate a smaller price rise or better terms while keeping the relationship.
Acknowledges the supplier's position and says you value the partnership.
Explains your position: a tight budget, several years as a loyal customer, and regular large orders.
Proposes specific options, such as a smaller or delayed increase, a volume discount, or a longer contract.
Uses a cooperative, polite and professional register.

items.situation: A long-standing client asks your team to finish their project a week earlier than agreed in the contract. Your team is already fully booked, and rushing the work would put its quality at risk. You do not want to lose this client, who is waiting for your answer on a video call. What would you say to the client?
key_points: Goal: politely refuse the earlier deadline while keeping the client satisfied.
Thanks the client and shows understanding of why they want the project sooner.
Explains honestly that the team is fully booked and rushing would put quality at risk.
Offers an alternative, such as delivering part of the work early or giving regular progress updates.
Uses a polite, formal register and ends on a positive note.

items.prompt: Smartphones are now part of almost every moment of our daily lives. Some people say they have made life much easier, while others feel they have pulled us away from family and friends. To what extent do you agree that smartphones have improved our daily lives?
key_points: Answers the exact question: how far smartphones have improved daily life overall.
States a clear position (agree, disagree or partly agree) and keeps it to the end.
Benefits: fast communication, maps, online payments and learning anywhere.
Drawbacks: distraction, less face-to-face time with family and friends, and too much screen time.
Weighs benefits against drawbacks, backs points with everyday examples, and ends with a clear conclusion.

items.prompt: Some people believe that living in a big city gives people a better life, while others think life in the countryside is better. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
key_points: Discusses both views: the case for city life and the case for country life.
Gives a clear personal opinion on which is better, not just a neutral list.
City side: more jobs, better schools and hospitals, and more entertainment and convenience.
Countryside side: cleaner air, less noise and traffic, lower living costs and closer communities.
Develops each side in its own paragraph with examples and links them to the final opinion.

items.prompt: Many people now buy clothes, food and household goods online instead of going to shops. What are the advantages and disadvantages of online shopping? Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
key_points: Answers both questions: the advantages and disadvantages, and whether the advantages outweigh them.
Gives a clear final judgement rather than only listing points.
Advantages: convenience, saving time, wider choice and easy price comparison.
Disadvantages: products cannot be seen or tried first, delivery and return problems, online scams, and harm to local shops.
Supports main points with specific examples, such as ordering clothes that do not fit.

items.prompt: Traffic jams are a daily problem in many large cities. What are the main causes of heavy traffic, and what can be done to reduce it?
key_points: Answers both parts: the main causes of heavy traffic and the solutions to reduce it.
Causes, e.g. too many private cars and motorbikes, weak public transport, poor city planning, and most people travelling at the same rush hours.
Solutions, e.g. better and cheaper public transport, limits or charges on private vehicles, and flexible working hours.
Links each solution to a cause and explains how it would work, with a concrete example such as a city the writer knows.
Ends with a clear conclusion that briefly restates the main causes and solutions.

items.prompt: Many busy people now eat fast food or order takeaway meals instead of cooking at home. Is this a positive or a negative development? Give reasons and examples to support your view.
key_points: Answers the exact question: whether replacing home cooking with fast food and takeaway is positive or negative.
States a clear position and keeps it consistent from introduction to conclusion.
Positive side: saves time for busy people, is convenient, and creates jobs in restaurants and delivery.
Negative side: often less healthy, costs more over time, and means fewer family meals together.
Supports the chosen side with specific examples and responds briefly to the other side.

items.prompt: Some people think that the main purpose of a university is to prepare students for jobs. Others believe it should give students broad knowledge and the ability to think for themselves. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
key_points: Discusses both views: university as job preparation and university as a place for broad knowledge and independent thinking.
Gives a clear personal opinion, which may be a reasoned balance between the two.
Job view: students need practical skills, employers want work-ready graduates, and a degree is a costly investment.
Knowledge view: thinking skills last longer than specific job skills, jobs keep changing, and society needs research and informed citizens.
Uses examples such as internships or subjects like philosophy and science, and concludes clearly.

items.prompt: Many companies now allow employees to work from home for part or all of the week. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this for employees and employers? Overall, do you think it is a positive change?
key_points: Answers all parts: advantages and disadvantages for both employees and employers, plus an overall judgement.
Gives a clear overall view, for example supporting a mix of home and office work.
Employees: no commute and more flexibility, but loneliness and a blurred line between work and home life.
Employers: lower office costs and access to workers from anywhere, but harder supervision, teamwork and communication.
Organises points clearly by group or by advantage and disadvantage, with concrete examples.

items.prompt: Many young people now spend a large part of their free time on social media. What problems can this cause, and what can parents and schools do to help?
key_points: Answers both parts: the problems caused by heavy social media use and what parents and schools can do.
Problems: less time for study, sleep and exercise, pressure from comparing themselves with others, and online bullying.
Parents, e.g. clear screen-time rules, phone-free family time, talking openly about online risks, and setting a good example.
Schools: teaching safe and responsible online behaviour, and offering sports and clubs as alternatives.
Explains how each suggested action would reduce a specific problem, and ends with a clear conclusion.

items.prompt: With the growth of online courses, some people believe that traditional classrooms will soon no longer be needed. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this view?
key_points: Answers the exact question: how far online courses could make traditional classrooms unnecessary.
States a clear position, for example that online learning will support classrooms but not fully replace them.
For online learning: flexible time and place, lower costs, and access to good teachers and materials from anywhere.
For classrooms: face-to-face interaction, motivation and discipline, hands-on practice, and social skills, especially for children.
Supports arguments with specific examples and concludes by restating the position.

items.prompt: When choosing a job, some people care most about the salary, while others think job satisfaction is more important. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
key_points: Discusses both views: salary as the top priority and job satisfaction as the top priority.
Gives a clear personal opinion, possibly noting that the answer depends on a person's situation.
Salary view: pays for living costs and family needs, gives financial security, and reflects the value of the work.
Satisfaction view: interest and meaning keep people motivated, reduce stress, and support long-term success and well-being.
Supports each side with realistic examples and ends with a clear conclusion.

items.prompt: Some argue that public funding for science should go only to research with clear practical applications. Others maintain that research driven purely by curiosity deserves government support as well. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
key_points: Discusses both views: funding only research with clear practical uses versus also funding curiosity-driven research.
Gives a clear, reasoned opinion on how public research money should be spent.
Practical view: public money is limited, taxpayers expect visible returns, and urgent problems such as disease need solutions.
Curiosity view: useful discoveries are often unexpected, basic knowledge underpins later applications, and private companies have little reason to fund it.
Supports arguments with a relevant example or careful reasoning, paraphrasing rather than repeating the prompt.

items.prompt: As trade, travel and digital media connect the world ever more closely, some fear that local cultures and traditions are being lost. To what extent do you agree that globalisation does more harm than good to local cultures?
key_points: Answers the exact question: whether globalisation does more harm than good to local cultures.
States a clear position and keeps it consistent, with nuance if partly agreeing.
Harm side: global brands, media and food can push aside local languages, crafts, food and customs.
Benefit side: cultural exchange, tourism that funds heritage, and the internet helping communities share and preserve traditions.
Supports points with specific examples, for instance from the writer's own country, and concludes clearly.

items.prompt: Technology companies collect vast amounts of personal data from the people who use their services. What problems does this practice create, and what measures should be taken to protect individual privacy?
key_points: Answers both parts: the problems of personal data collection and the measures to protect privacy.
Problems: loss of privacy, data leaks and misuse, manipulation through targeted content, and users not knowing what is collected.
Measures, e.g. strong data protection laws with real penalties, clear consent, collecting only necessary data, and users managing their own privacy settings.
Links each measure to a problem it solves and explains how it would work.
Supports points with concrete examples, such as targeted advertising or a data leak, and ends with a clear conclusion.

items.prompt: Some argue that protecting the natural environment must take priority over economic growth, even if this means slower development and fewer jobs in the short term. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
key_points: Answers the exact question: whether protecting the environment should come first, even at the cost of slower growth and fewer jobs in the short term.
States a clear position on how far the writer agrees, not only that both matter.
Environment-first case: damage such as pollution and climate change is costly or impossible to reverse, and future generations depend on healthy nature.
Growth case: poorer countries need development to reduce poverty, and wealth helps pay for cleaner technology.
Responds to the opposing side, for example by showing how green industries can create jobs, and supports points with examples.

items.prompt: Artificial intelligence is now able to assist with high-stakes decisions such as selecting job applicants, diagnosing illnesses and approving bank loans. What are the advantages and disadvantages of relying on artificial intelligence for such decisions? Do the benefits outweigh the risks?
key_points: Answers both questions: the advantages and disadvantages of relying on AI for important decisions, and whether the benefits outweigh the risks.
Gives a clear overall judgement, for example that AI should support, not replace, human judgement.
Advantages: speed, ability to process large amounts of data, consistency, and lower costs.
Disadvantages: bias learned from past data, decisions that are hard to explain or challenge, privacy concerns, and unclear responsibility for mistakes.
Uses at least one of the named areas (hiring, medicine or loans) as a concrete example.
